practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines a natural hazard?
A) Any event in the natural environment
B) An event in the natural environment that has the potential to cause harm to people or property
C) An event caused only by human activity
D) An event that happens only at plate boundaries
practice_questions.marks: B) An event in the natural environment that has the potential to cause harm to people or property [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two factors that affect hazard risk.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per factor identified with brief development. Examples: population density (more people in danger zone increase exposure); wealth (richer places afford warning systems and stronger buildings); frequency (regular hazards lead to better preparation); type of hazard (some give more warning than others).

practice_questions.text: Describe the global distribution of earthquakes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear pattern with two named locations and use of compass direction (e.g. 'concentrated along the western and eastern edges of the Pacific, including Japan and Chile, and across the Mediterranean into the Himalayas'). Secure: pattern identified with one named example. Developing: a vague pattern with no place name. Emerging: simple statement that earthquakes happen 'in lots of places'.

practice_questions.text: Explain how convection currents in the mantle move tectonic plates.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — heat from the core warms the mantle, hot rock rises, cools near the crust, sinks again, and the circulating current drags plates above. Secure: heat causes mantle movement and this moves plates, with one mechanism named. Developing: links heat to plate movement but skips the convection step. Emerging: states that the mantle is hot but does not link to plates.

practice_questions.text: Compare oceanic and continental crust.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three points of comparison using comparative language (denser, thinner, younger), supported by an example such as the Pacific (oceanic) vs the Eurasian land mass (continental). Secure: two points of comparison with comparative connectives. Developing: lists features of each separately without comparing. Emerging: only one feature named with no comparison.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that hazard risk depends mostly on a country's wealth.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a balanced argument acknowledging that wealth is important (warning systems, building codes reduce death toll, e.g. Japan vs Haiti) but evaluating that population density, hazard type and frequency also matter, reaching a justified judgement (e.g. wealth is the most modifiable factor but not the only one). Secure: balanced argument with one or two factors weighed against wealth. Developing: lists factors with limited evaluation or judgement. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines a megacity?
A) A capital city of any country
B) A city with a population of 10 million or more
C) A city in a high-income country
D) A city growing by more than 5% per year
practice_questions.marks: B) A city with a population of 10 million or more [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two pull factors that draw rural migrants into LIC cities.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per factor identified with brief development. Examples: paid factory or service jobs (more reliable income than subsistence farming); better access to hospitals and schools; mains water and electricity; the chance of a better future for children.

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of megacity growth since 1970.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: pattern stated with named places and direction (e.g. 'in 1970 only Tokyo, New York and Osaka were megacities; today over thirty exist, with most growth in Asia such as Delhi and Africa such as Lagos, while HIC megacities are stable'). Secure: pattern with one named example. Developing: vague statement that there are 'more big cities now'. Emerging: simple claim of growth with no places.

practice_questions.text: Explain how natural increase contributes to urban growth in LICs and NEEs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — recent migrants are young adults, they have children in the city, urban clinics and clean water cut the infant death rate, so births stay high while deaths fall and the population grows from within. Secure: links young migrants to higher births and lower deaths but misses one step. Developing: states there are more births than deaths but no link to migrants or services. Emerging: states people have children but does not link to urban growth.

practice_questions.text: Compare the pattern of urban growth in HICs and LICs/NEEs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three points of comparison using comparative connectives (whereas, in contrast). HICs grew fastest during the Industrial Revolution and are now stable or counter-urbanising (London, Tokyo); LICs/NEEs are still in their first wave of rapid growth driven by migration and natural increase (Lagos, Delhi). Secure: two points of comparison with named places. Developing: features listed separately without comparing. Emerging: only one feature with no comparison.

practice_questions.text: Assess the relative importance of rural-to-urban migration and natural increase as causes of LIC city growth.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named places and a justified judgement — migration provides the initial young population pulled by factory jobs in cities like Lagos, but natural increase becomes dominant once those migrants settle, lowering death rates and raising survival of children. Conclusion weighs the two and reaches a judgement (e.g. 'migration triggers the growth, natural increase sustains it'). Secure: both causes explained with one named example, modest evaluation. Developing: describes both without weighing them. Emerging: describes one cause only or lists factors without explanation. [9 marks plus up to 3 SPaG marks where applicable]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes a destructive plate margin?
A) Two plates moving apart, creating new crust
B) Two plates sliding past each other horizontally
C) Two plates moving together, with one subducting beneath the other
D) Two plates that have stopped moving
practice_questions.marks: C) Two plates moving together, with one subducting beneath the other [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what happens at a conservative plate margin.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for identifying horizontal sliding past each other. 1 mark for development — e.g. 'no crust is created or destroyed' or 'friction locks plates and releases earthquakes'. Named example (San Andreas) accepted as development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two reasons why people choose to live in hazard zones.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two reasons clearly described with location-specific detail (e.g. 'fertile volcanic soil supports farming around Mount Vesuvius' and 'jobs in cities like Tokyo'). Secure: two reasons with one example. Developing: two reasons but vague. Emerging: only one reason or generic statements.

practice_questions.text: Explain why volcanoes form at destructive plate margins but not at conservative margins.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal explanation — at destructive margins the descending oceanic plate melts in the mantle, magma rises and erupts; at conservative margins no plate is subducted so no melting and no magma. Secure: identifies subduction at destructive but not conservative. Developing: vaguely states 'one has volcanoes, one doesn't' without mechanism. Emerging: confuses the two margin types.

practice_questions.text: Compare the hazards found at constructive and destructive plate margins.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three comparisons using comparative connectives (whereas, in contrast) covering volcanic style (effusive vs explosive), earthquake size (small vs large), and crust process (created vs destroyed). Named examples for each (Iceland, Andes). Secure: two clear comparisons with examples. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: confuses or describes only one type.

practice_questions.text: 'People should not be allowed to live in tectonic hazard zones.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with for and against points (lives at risk, cost of disasters vs. fertile soil, geothermal energy, jobs, family ties), uses named places (Naples, Iceland, San Andreas) and reaches a justified judgement — e.g. that managing risk is more practical than relocation. Secure: balanced argument with one or two examples. Developing: one-sided or limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is true of Lagos?
A) It is the political capital of Nigeria
B) It has a population of around 1 million
C) It is on Nigeria's south-west Atlantic coast
D) It is the only NEE city in West Africa
practice_questions.marks: C) It is on Nigeria's south-west Atlantic coast [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why Lagos is regionally and nationally important.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: it produces around 30% of Nigeria's GDP; Apapa port handles roughly 70% of Nigeria's sea trade; it hosts multinational companies such as Nestlé and Unilever; Murtala Muhammed Airport is West Africa's busiest hub.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location and importance of Lagos using the case study you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: precise location (south-west Atlantic coast of Nigeria, on lagoons) and importance with named example (around 16 million people, 30% of Nigerian GDP, hosts Nollywood). Secure: location stated with one importance fact. Developing: location vague but one importance point given. Emerging: 'a big city in Africa' with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain how rural-to-urban migration has caused the rapid growth of Lagos.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — push factors such as drought in the Sahel and Boko Haram conflict in the north-east force people off the land; pull factors such as port jobs at Apapa and the chance of better healthcare draw them in; around 2,000 arrive daily, swelling the population. Secure: links push and pull factors to migration into Lagos with one named place or figure. Developing: lists factors without linking to migration. Emerging: states people move to Lagos for jobs.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how urban growth has created economic opportunities for the people of Lagos.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three opportunities developed with named places — e.g. dock and freight work at Apapa port (70% of Nigerian sea trade), factory work for multinationals such as Nestlé and Unilever in Ikeja, financial sector roles in Eko Atlantic, and the informal economy of okadas and street trading. Secure: two opportunities with one named example each. Developing: two opportunities described in general terms only. Emerging: one opportunity, no detail.

practice_questions.text: Assess the extent to which urban growth in Lagos has created opportunities for its residents.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a balanced argument with named places, recognising that opportunities are real but unequal — new arrivals in Apapa, Ikeja or Eko Atlantic earn three to four times rural wages; healthcare and education stretch further than any village; but most rely on the informal economy and not all benefit. Justified judgement reached. Secure: opportunities described with two named examples and modest evaluation. Developing: opportunities listed without weighing them. Emerging: opportunities listed in general only. [9 marks plus up to 3 SPaG marks where applicable]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a primary effect of an earthquake?
A) Disease spreading in displacement camps
B) Buildings collapsing during the shaking
C) Long-term economic decline
D) Tourists cancelling visits in the months afterwards
practice_questions.marks: B) Buildings collapsing during the shaking [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two secondary effects of the 2015 Nepal earthquake.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per effect with brief development. Examples: avalanches on Everest killed 19 climbers; cholera outbreaks in displacement camps; loss of around a third of GDP; long-term homelessness for 3 million.

practice_questions.text: Describe the immediate responses to the 2011 Christchurch earthquake.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear description with at least two named responses (Civil Defence within minutes, international SAR teams, power restored in 5 days). Secure: two responses identified. Developing: one response with little detail. Emerging: vague reference to 'help arriving'.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the death toll was much higher in Nepal than in Christchurch despite both being earthquakes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: causal chain — Nepal had weaker buildings (mud-mortar, brick) that collapsed easily; limited warning systems; poor road access slowed rescue; New Zealand had strict building codes, education, fast Civil Defence. At least two factors with explanation. Secure: two factors but only partly explained. Developing: one factor or vague comparison. Emerging: 'Nepal is poorer' without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: Compare the long-term recovery in Nepal and Christchurch.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three comparative points covering rebuilding speed (slow vs fast), funding source (international aid vs government/insurance), quality of rebuild (uneven enforcement vs higher seismic standards), with named places. Secure: two comparisons with examples. Developing: lists features separately. Emerging: only describes one place.

practice_questions.text: 'A country's wealth has more impact than the magnitude of an earthquake on its effects.' Assess this view using the Nepal and Christchurch case studies.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with evidence from both case studies, weighing wealth (codes, services, recovery) against the role of magnitude, depth and proximity to settlement. Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. wealth is the dominant lever in saving lives, but a large enough magnitude can still overwhelm any country). Secure: balanced argument with evidence. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best definition of a squatter settlement?
A) A planned urban district built by the government
B) Housing built informally on land the residents do not own
C) A high-rise apartment block in a wealthy area
D) A gated community on the city edge
practice_questions.marks: B) Housing built informally on land the residents do not own [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two challenges of providing clean water in Lagos.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per challenge with brief development. Examples: only around 10% of Lagos has a reliable mains supply, so most residents buy from tankers or sachets at higher cost; less than 10% is on a working sewer so untreated waste contaminates lagoon water; population grows faster than infrastructure can be extended; cholera and typhoid outbreaks recur most years.

practice_questions.text: Describe the conditions in the Makoko slum in Lagos.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: precise detail with figures — 100,000–250,000 residents, stilt houses on a lagoon polluted by sewage and sawmill waste, no formal land title, no mains water. Secure: two specific features named. Developing: vague description as 'a poor area'. Emerging: states it is a slum with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain how rapid population growth has caused environmental problems in Lagos.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — 13,000 tonnes of daily waste outpaces collection, dumps such as Olusosun catch fire and pollute the air; sewers cover under 10% of homes so untreated waste reaches Lagos Lagoon; traffic in the 'go-slow' burns fuel and worsens PM2.5 pollution. Secure: links growth to two environmental issues with one named place. Developing: links growth to pollution in general terms. Emerging: lists pollution issues with no link to growth.

practice_questions.text: Suggest the social challenges created by urban growth in a NEE megacity you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three social challenges developed with named places — informal housing in Makoko, overcrowded schools (classes of 80), under-staffed clinics in slum areas, crime concentrated in poorer districts ('area boys'). Each linked to rapid growth. Secure: two social challenges with named example each. Developing: two challenges in general terms. Emerging: one challenge listed without detail.

practice_questions.text: 'Environmental challenges are the most serious problem facing Lagos.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named evidence on both sides — for the statement: 13,000 tonnes of daily waste, the burning Olusosun landfill, polluted Lagos Lagoon, the go-slow. Against: housing crisis (Makoko, two-thirds in slums), service gaps (10% mains water, less than 10% sewers), unemployment and crime. Justified judgement weighing them. Secure: two challenges from different categories with modest evaluation. Developing: lists challenges without weighing them. Emerging: describes one category of challenge only. [9 marks plus up to 3 SPaG marks where applicable]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a self-help scheme?
A) A government-funded high-rise housing block
B) A community-led project where residents help to improve their own neighbourhood
C) A police-led anti-crime initiative
D) A privately-owned shopping mall
practice_questions.marks: B) A community-led project where residents help to improve their own neighbourhood [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of the Makoko Floating School that made it sustainable.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature with brief development. Examples: 256 recycled plastic barrels for buoyancy (re-using waste); solar panels providing electricity (no fossil fuels); rainwater collection (independent of mains supply); built with locally-sourced wood and Makoko community labour.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Lagos Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) scheme.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: precise detail — opened in 2008, uses lanes separated from general traffic so buses bypass the 'go-slow', low fares accessible to low-income workers, journey times cut by up to half on some routes. Secure: two specific features named. Developing: vague description as 'a bus system'. Emerging: states it is public transport with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain how self-help schemes can improve quality of life for the urban poor in Lagos.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — community-led projects such as the Makoko Floating School build classrooms in places without dry land, NGO-run boreholes (WaterAid) supply safer drinking water in slums, Solar Sister provides clean lighting that replaces kerosene smoke. Each links to better health, education and incomes. Secure: links one self-help scheme to one quality-of-life improvement. Developing: lists schemes without explaining the link. Emerging: names a scheme but does not link to quality of life.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how a named project is improving the quality of life for the urban poor in a NEE megacity you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points with named example. Strongest answers use the Makoko Floating School (2013, Kunlé Adeyemi, 256 plastic barrels, 100 pupils, solar power, rainwater harvesting, built with community) and link to a clear quality-of-life gain (education access, sustainable design, community pride). Could also use BRT or Solar Sister. Secure: three points with one named example. Developing: two points described in general terms. Emerging: one point with no name.

practice_questions.text: 'Top-down government schemes are more effective than community-led self-help in improving life for the urban poor.' Evaluate this statement using a named NEE city.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named evidence on both sides. For: BRT, Lagos Rail and Eko Atlantic City deliver scale and infrastructure that NGOs alone cannot. Against: top-down projects such as Eko Atlantic mostly serve the wealthy, while self-help reaches slum communities — the Makoko Floating School and WaterAid boreholes deliver direct benefits to the urban poor. Justified judgement (e.g. 'most effective when both work together'). Secure: examples on both sides with modest evaluation. Developing: lists examples without weighing. Emerging: one approach described only. [9 marks plus up to 3 SPaG marks where applicable]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of monitoring?
A) Building a tsunami sea wall
B) Drawing a hazard map for a city
C) Tracking gas emissions from a volcano
D) Running an earthquake drill in a school
practice_questions.marks: C) Tracking gas emissions from a volcano [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways volcanoes are monitored.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per method with development. Examples: seismometers detect tremors caused by rising magma; GPS sensors spot ground bulging as magma fills the chamber; gas sniffers detect sulphur dioxide which rises before eruptions.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways buildings can be designed to withstand earthquakes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two methods clearly described with how they work (e.g. base isolators — rubber pads beneath buildings absorb shaking; reinforced concrete frames flex without breaking). Secure: two methods named. Developing: one method or vague. Emerging: 'make them stronger' with no specifics.

practice_questions.text: Explain why earthquake prediction is more difficult than volcanic prediction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear contrast — volcanoes give detectable warning signs (tremors, gas, ground deformation) over hours or days; earthquakes strike suddenly with no reliable precursor. Causal explanation that earthquake fault stress is not visible like rising magma is. Secure: identifies the contrast with one mechanism. Developing: states one is harder without explaining. Emerging: confuses the two hazards.

practice_questions.text: Suggest why high-income countries are usually better at managing tectonic hazards than low-income countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three reasons explained, covering technology (warning systems), building codes (enforcement), emergency services (training and equipment), and education (drills). Named example such as Japan or New Zealand. Secure: two reasons with examples. Developing: lists reasons without explanation. Emerging: 'they have more money' alone.

practice_questions.text: 'Protection is the most effective way to manage tectonic hazards.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument weighing protection (earthquake-resistant buildings save lives directly) against monitoring/prediction (give time to evacuate volcanoes) and planning (drills and routes co-ordinate response). Reaches a justified conclusion that the four Ps work together; protection saves the most lives but only when combined with planning. Use of named examples (Tokyo, Japan, San Andreas). Secure: balanced with two factors. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Tropical storms in the western Pacific Ocean are called:
A) Hurricanes
B) Typhoons
C) Cyclones
D) Tornadoes
practice_questions.marks: B) Typhoons [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two conditions needed for a tropical storm to form.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per condition with brief development. Examples: ocean water above 26.5°C providing energy; the Coriolis effect to make the storm spin (away from the equator); low wind shear so the storm is not torn apart; unstable atmosphere allowing rapid air rise.

practice_questions.text: Describe the global distribution of tropical storms.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear pattern using latitude (5–30° north and south of the equator) and at least two named regions (Caribbean/Atlantic, western Pacific, Indian Ocean). Notes that they avoid the equator itself. Secure: latitude band with one example. Developing: 'tropical areas' without latitudes. Emerging: vague reference to 'hot places'.

practice_questions.text: Explain how warm ocean water leads to the formation of a tropical storm.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — warm water heats the air above it; warm moist air rises rapidly; rising air cools and condenses, releasing latent heat; latent heat warms the surrounding air, accelerating the rise and drawing in more air from the sea. Secure: identifies rising air and condensation. Developing: 'water gives energy' without mechanism. Emerging: 'heat causes storms' alone.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how climate change might affect tropical storms in the future.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three suggestions explained — greater intensity (warmer water = more energy), expanded range (storms reaching higher latitudes as more oceans cross 26.5°C), longer season, possibly fewer but stronger storms. Use of 'might' or 'could' acknowledging uncertainty. Secure: two effects with explanation. Developing: lists effects without explanation. Emerging: 'storms get worse' alone.

practice_questions.text: Assess the role of the global atmospheric circulation in shaping the world's climate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument using the model (low at equator, high at 30°, low at 60°) to explain rainforest, desert and temperate climates with named examples (Amazon, Sahara, UK). Reaches a justified judgement that circulation is the dominant control on global climate, while acknowledging local factors (ocean currents, altitude, continentality). Secure: explains the model with examples. Developing: lists pressure belts without linking to climates. Emerging: vague reference to 'wind moving heat'.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the UK’s population distribution?
A) Evenly spread across all regions
B) Concentrated in lowland areas, the south-east and old industrial cities
C) Concentrated in the Scottish Highlands and mid-Wales
D) Mainly rural with very few large cities
practice_questions.marks: B) Concentrated in lowland areas, the south-east and old industrial cities [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why parts of upland Britain have a low population density.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: steep relief in the Scottish Highlands or Lake District makes building difficult; cold and wet upland climates shorten growing seasons; thin moorland soils cannot support large-scale farming; few jobs since mining and traditional farming declined.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location of a major UK city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: precise location with compass direction and reference points (e.g. 'Manchester is in north-west England, about 50 km east of Liverpool, in the lowlands at the confluence of three rivers'). Secure: location with one reference point. Developing: vague placement ('in the north'). Emerging: city named with no location detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Manchester is important within the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two developed reasons — e.g. it is a major financial centre with banks and law firms based at Spinningfields, supporting tens of thousands of professional jobs; it has four universities (including the University of Manchester) attracting students nationally and globally and feeding the regional economy with skilled workers. Secure: two reasons each with one named example. Developing: lists features without explaining importance. Emerging: states one reason with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why a UK city you have studied is important on the world stage.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points with named features. Strongest answers cover sport (Manchester United and Manchester City watched globally), media (MediaCityUK / BBC), research (Sir Henry Royce Institute, graphene), aviation (Manchester Airport, third-busiest in the UK with 200+ destinations) and education (international students). Secure: three points with one named example. Developing: two general points. Emerging: one point with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Assess how far physical and human factors together explain the UK’s uneven population distribution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named places. Physical: relief (Highlands, Snowdonia, Lake District), upland climate, poor soils push density down. Human: industrial heritage (Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, Sheffield), London’s pull as a financial capital, university towns and good transport links pull density up. Justified judgement that physical factors set the limits, human factors explain where within those limits people cluster. Secure: both physical and human factors with named places. Developing: one factor type only. Emerging: lists places without linking to factors. [9 marks plus up to 3 SPaG marks where applicable]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes urban deprivation?
A) When a city has too many tourists
B) When residents lack basic resources and opportunities such as good housing, health care and work
C) When new commuter villages grow on the city edge
D) When industries move out of a city
practice_questions.marks: B) When residents lack basic resources and opportunities such as good housing, health care and work [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two opportunities that international migration has created in Manchester.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per opportunity with brief development. Examples: cultural mix shown by the Curry Mile in Rusholme and Manchester's Chinatown; festivals such as the Caribbean Carnival; staffing for the NHS by overseas-trained doctors and nurses; entrepreneurship and small businesses founded by migrant families.

practice_questions.text: Describe the pattern of urban deprivation in a major UK city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: precise pattern with named wards and statistic — e.g. 'Manchester has some of the most deprived wards in England, including Harpurhey, Gorton and Ardwick, where life expectancy can be around seven years lower than in wealthier suburbs'. Secure: pattern with one named ward. Developing: vague description as 'some areas are poorer'. Emerging: states deprivation exists with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain how national migration has changed the size and character of a UK city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — Manchester's universities attract around 100,000 students, many of whom stay after graduation; families and professionals move north from London because housing is cheaper; the BBC's MediaCityUK move drew broadcasting jobs; together these have grown the population and changed the demographic profile. Secure: links one or two groups to changes in the city. Developing: states migrants come without explaining the impact. Emerging: notes population growth without naming groups.

practice_questions.text: Suggest the social, economic and environmental challenges urban growth has created in a UK city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three challenges from different categories with named places. Social: deprivation in Harpurhey/Gorton/Ardwick, life-expectancy gap, education attainment gaps. Economic: housing affordability, jobs needing degrees, council waiting lists. Environmental: urban sprawl into Trafford and Stockport, traffic and air pollution, pressure on green belt. Secure: three challenges with one named place. Developing: two challenges in general terms. Emerging: one challenge with no detail.

practice_questions.text: 'International migration brings more opportunities than challenges to a UK city.' Evaluate this statement using a named UK city.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named evidence on both sides. Opportunities: cultural mix (Curry Mile, Chinatown, Caribbean Carnival), NHS staffing, entrepreneurship, food and creative industries. Challenges: housing pressure, school capacity, integration costs, deprivation in some migrant-heavy wards. Justified judgement reached. Secure: examples on both sides with modest evaluation. Developing: lists examples without weighing. Emerging: one side described only. [9 marks plus up to 3 SPaG marks where applicable]

practice_questions.text:
What category was Hurricane Ida at landfall?
A) Category 1
B) Category 2
C) Category 4
D) Category 5
practice_questions.marks: C) Category 4 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two secondary effects of Hurricane Ida.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per effect with development. Examples: record rainfall and flash flooding in New York and New Jersey; people drowning in basement flats; power outages lasting weeks; ~$75 billion economic damage; subway flooding.

practice_questions.text: Describe the path Hurricane Ida took.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear path with at least three locations and direction (formed near Jamaica, intensified over Caribbean, made landfall in Louisiana, weakened then re-intensified rainfall over north-east US). Secure: two locations. Developing: vague path. Emerging: only mentions one place.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Hurricane Ida intensified so rapidly before landfall.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: causal chain — sea-surface temperatures around 30°C provided abundant energy; warm moist air rose rapidly; condensation released latent heat that accelerated rising air; low wind shear allowed the storm to organise. Secure: warm sea + organised structure. Developing: 'sea was warm' alone. Emerging: 'storms always get bigger'.

practice_questions.text: Compare the immediate and long-term responses to Hurricane Ida.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three contrasts — immediate (mandatory evacuation, National Guard, FEMA, emergency shelters) vs long-term (rebuild, insurance pay-outs, new NYC flood-proofing rules, infrastructure investment). Comparative connectives. Secure: two contrasts. Developing: lists separately. Emerging: only describes one.

practice_questions.text: 'Hurricane Ida shows that high-income countries are still vulnerable to tropical storms.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with evidence — HICs are better prepared (early warning, evacuations, insurance) but Ida still killed ~100 people and caused $75 billion in damage. Vulnerability comes from old infrastructure, climate-change-fuelled rainfall, and densely populated low-lying cities. Justified judgement that wealth reduces but does not eliminate risk. Secure: balanced with evidence. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines a brownfield site?
A) Land that has never been built on
B) Land that has previously been built on, often in inner cities
C) Farmland on the edge of a city
D) Protected green belt land
practice_questions.marks: B) Land that has previously been built on, often in inner cities [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two benefits of urban greening for city residents.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per benefit with brief development. Examples: lowers urban temperatures by several degrees in summer, reducing heat-related illness; traps fine particulate air pollution near busy roads; reduces surface flooding because vegetation lets rain soak in; improves mental health and physical activity by giving residents access to parks; supports urban biodiversity such as bees and birds.

practice_questions.text: Describe the main features of an urban regeneration project you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: precise detail with named features — Salford Quays on the closed Manchester Ship Canal docks, including MediaCityUK, the Lowry Centre, the Imperial War Museum North and around 5,000 new homes. Secure: two named features. Developing: vague description as 'flats and shops were built'. Emerging: project named with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why an inner-city area needed regeneration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — e.g. Salford Quays was the busy inland end of the Manchester Ship Canal until containerisation in the 1970s sent shipping to deeper-water ports; this caused around 3,000 dock jobs to close, basins to fill with debris, warehouses to fall derelict and water to become polluted, leaving the area economically and environmentally damaged. Secure: links one cause to one effect with a named place. Developing: states there were derelict buildings without explaining why. Emerging: notes the area was poor with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how brownfield development and urban greening together improve quality of life in a UK city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points combining the two strategies. Brownfield: Salford Quays brings jobs, homes and culture to a previously derelict area. Greening: Mayfield Park (6.5 acres, opened 2022 on former rail land), green roofs at MediaCityUK and Metrolink-supported reductions in car use. Each linked to specific quality-of-life gain — jobs, lower pollution, mental health, lower flood risk. Secure: three points with one named example. Developing: two general points. Emerging: one point with no detail.

practice_questions.text: Assess the extent to which urban regeneration and urban greening have improved life in a UK city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named evidence. Successes: Salford Quays jobs and homes, Mayfield Park and other green space, Metrolink expansion cutting car use. Limits: regeneration can raise rents and displace lower-income residents, deprivation persists in wards like Harpurhey and Gorton, sprawl into the rural-urban fringe continues, building enough new homes is slow. Justified judgement weighing visible improvements against persisting inequalities. Secure: examples on both sides with modest evaluation. Developing: lists improvements without weighing limits. Emerging: improvements only, no evaluation. [9 marks plus up to 3 SPaG marks where applicable]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a recent UK heatwave landmark?
A) The UK passed 40°C for the first time in 2022
B) The UK passed 50°C in 2018
C) The UK had its coldest winter on record in 2010
D) The Beast from the East struck in 2024
practice_questions.marks: A) The UK passed 40°C for the first time in 2022 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two types of weather hazard experienced in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per hazard with brief development. Examples: storms (Atlantic depressions bringing strong winds, e.g. Storm Eunice); floods (e.g. Cumbria 2015); heatwaves (40°C in July 2022); droughts (July 2022 the driest July in England since 1935); snow/ice events (Beast from the East 2018).

practice_questions.text: Describe the impacts of Storm Desmond on Cumbria.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three impacts with figures and named places (5,200 homes flooded, 2,200 in Carlisle, hospital evacuated, £500 million damage). Secure: two impacts with figures. Developing: vague mention of flooding. Emerging: 'people lost their homes' alone.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Storm Desmond produced such extreme rainfall.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: causal chain — an atmospheric river of tropical moisture; orographic rainfall as moist air was forced over the Lake District mountains; saturated ground from previous rain; warmer Atlantic waters (climate change) holding more vapour. At least two factors with mechanism. Secure: two factors named. Developing: 'lots of rain fell' without mechanism. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how UK weather is changing as a result of climate change.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three suggestions explained — more frequent and intense rain (Desmond), record-breaking heat (40°C 2022), expanded heatwave range, drier summers and droughts. Cited evidence (Met Office: winters about 13% wetter than in 1961–1990). Secure: two changes with evidence. Developing: lists changes without evidence. Emerging: 'weather gets worse' alone.

practice_questions.text: 'Climate change is the main reason UK weather hazards are becoming more extreme.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging that climate change drives more intense rainfall and higher temperatures (citing Desmond and 40°C event), while also weighing in other factors — urban land use change, ageing flood defences, more people living in floodplains. Reaches a justified judgement. Secure: balanced with evidence. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of mitigation?
A) Building higher sea walls
B) Replacing coal power stations with wind farms
C) Breeding drought-resistant crops
D) Planning evacuation routes for tropical storms
practice_questions.marks: B) Replacing coal power stations with wind farms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two natural causes of climate change.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per cause with brief development. Examples: orbital changes (Milankovitch cycles alter sunlight reaching Earth, drive ice ages); volcanic activity (large eruptions can cool the planet for years, e.g. Tambora 1815); solar output variation (sunspot cycles affect incoming energy).

practice_questions.text: Describe two pieces of evidence that climate is changing today.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two evidence types described with detail (e.g. ice cores show CO₂ rising from 280 to 420 ppm; thermometer records show ~1°C global rise since 1850). Secure: two pieces of evidence named. Developing: one piece. Emerging: vague reference to 'getting hotter'.

practice_questions.text: Explain how burning fossil fuels causes climate change.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — burning releases carbon dioxide; CO₂ is a greenhouse gas; it absorbs infrared from the Earth's surface and re-emits it back, trapping heat; the atmosphere warms; this raises global temperatures. Secure: identifies CO₂ and greenhouse effect. Developing: 'pollution heats the air'. Emerging: 'fossil fuels are bad'.

practice_questions.text: Compare mitigation and adaptation strategies for managing climate change.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three contrasts — aim (prevent vs cope), examples (renewables/Paris Agreement vs sea walls/drought crops), timescale (long-term vs immediate), cost-bearer (global vs local). Comparative connectives. Secure: two contrasts with examples. Developing: lists separately. Emerging: only describes one.

practice_questions.text: 'Mitigation is more important than adaptation in managing climate change.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging mitigation's role (without it, future warming and damage are unbounded) while recognising adaptation's necessity (some warming is already locked in; vulnerable countries need defences now). Cited examples (Paris Agreement; Maldives sea defences). Justified judgement that both are essential, with reasons. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a feature of sustainable urban living?
A) Building only on greenfield sites
B) Recycling household waste
C) Increasing landfill use
D) Banning public transport
practice_questions.marks: B) Recycling household waste [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline one way water can be conserved in a sustainable urban area.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a method (water meter / low-flush toilet / rainwater harvesting / grey water recycling) plus 1 mark for explaining how it conserves water (e.g. meters mean households pay only for what they use, so they cut waste; rainwater butts catch roof runoff to water gardens). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how creating green space contributes to sustainable urban living.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for describing benefits of urban green space:
• Cools the city by 2–4°C in summer (reduces heat-island effect)
• Absorbs rainwater, reducing flood risk
• Absorbs CO₂ and air pollution from traffic
• Boosts mental health and wellbeing of residents
• Supports biodiversity in cities
[3 marks — 1 mark per developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain how urban transport strategies can reduce traffic congestion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation linking at least two named strategies (e.g. ULEZ, Bee Network, congestion charging) to clear mechanisms by which they reduce car use.
Secure: Two strategies explained with clear reasoning — e.g. integrated tickets make buses cheaper and easier so drivers switch from cars; congestion charges make driving in central London expensive so people use the Tube instead.
Developing: Strategies named but only briefly explained.
Emerging: Lists strategies without explaining how they cut congestion.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Compare two strategies a UK city could use to become more sustainable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed comparison of two named strategies using comparative connectives (whereas, in contrast, similarly), with examples and weighing which is more effective.
Secure: Two strategies clearly compared (e.g. ULEZ targets transport pollution whereas BedZED tackles housing energy use; both cut emissions but ULEZ acts faster while BedZED has lower long-term costs).
Developing: Two strategies described but compared only loosely.
Emerging: One strategy described or both listed without comparison.
Indicative content: ULEZ vs cycle highways, BedZED vs urban greening, recycling schemes vs water metering, integrated transport vs park-and-ride.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Smart transport strategies are the most effective way to make UK cities sustainable.’
Assess this statement.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Sustained assessment that weighs transport strategies against other sustainability features (water, energy, waste, green space). Uses named UK evidence (ULEZ cut inner-London NOx by around 20%; BedZED is carbon-neutral; London targets 50% green by 2050). Reaches a clear judgement.
Secure (5–6): Both sides argued with named examples; some weighing of importance; conclusion attempts a judgement.
Developing (3–4): Lists strategies on each side but limited evidence and no clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2): One-sided answer or general comments without examples.
+3 SPaG marks awarded separately.
Indicative content: FOR — transport is biggest source of urban air pollution and ULEZ shows fast results; AGAINST — energy use in buildings is larger overall, recycling reduces resource demand, green space tackles flooding and heat; JUDGEMENT — most effective approach combines all four features. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a producer?
A) A water flea
B) A heron
C) Algae
D) A pond bacterium
practice_questions.marks: C) Algae [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for breaking down dead organic matter; 1 mark for development e.g. returning nutrients to the soil so plants can re-use them.

practice_questions.text: Describe the abiotic and biotic components of a UK pond ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three components named, split correctly between biotic (algae, sticklebacks, herons, bacteria) and abiotic (water, dissolved oxygen, sunlight, mud). Secure: two components correctly placed. Developing: components named without distinction. Emerging: 'a pond has fish' alone.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a pollution event might disrupt the balance of a pond ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — e.g. fertiliser runoff increases nutrients; algae bloom; bloom blocks sunlight; deeper plants die; their decomposition uses oxygen; fish suffocate. Secure: identifies bloom and oxygen loss. Developing: vague reference to 'fish dying'. Emerging: 'pollution is bad'.

practice_questions.text: Compare the climates of tropical rainforest and tundra biomes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three contrasts using comparative language — latitude (equatorial vs near Arctic), temperature (hot vs cold), rainfall (very wet vs very low/seasonal), vegetation (tall trees vs treeless), biodiversity (very high vs low). Secure: two contrasts. Developing: lists features separately. Emerging: only describes one biome.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that all ecosystems — from a small pond to a global biome — share the same fundamental components.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument confirming shared structure (producers, consumers, decomposers, biotic-abiotic interactions, nutrient cycling) but acknowledging genuine differences (scale, biodiversity, climate range, vulnerability). Reaches a justified judgement, e.g. that the principles are universal but their expression is highly varied. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: agrees or disagrees with limited evidence. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a social indicator of development?
A) GNI per head
B) Infant mortality rate
C) Inflation rate
D) Exports of manufactured goods
practice_questions.marks: B) Infant mortality rate [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what the Human Development Index (HDI) measures.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying HDI as a composite measure / score 0–1; 1 mark for naming at least one of its three components (life expectancy, education / years of schooling, GNI per head). Full marks for capturing that HDI combines income, health and education into a single score. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the changes in birth rate and death rate during Stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Death rate falls sharply (1 mark)
• Reasons: better food, clean water, vaccinations, medicine (1 mark for explanation)
• Birth rate remains high so population grows rapidly (1 mark)
Alternative full-credit answer: gap between high birth rate and falling death rate widens, causing fast population growth. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two limitations of using GNI per head as a measure of development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two limitations clearly explained with developed reasoning.
Secure: Two limitations identified and explained — e.g. 'GNI per head is an average, so a few wealthy people can mask widespread poverty among the majority' / 'It does not capture the informal economy, which provides ~70% of jobs in much of Africa, so true earnings are higher than the figure shows' / 'It says nothing about how income is spent — a country may have high GNI but poor schools and healthcare'.
Developing: Two points named but only one well explained.
Emerging: Lists limitations without explaining why each matters.
[4 marks — 2 marks per limitation]

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why a country in Stage 3 of the Demographic Transition Model has a falling birth rate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Several developed reasons connected with examples or evidence; clear chains of explanation.
Secure: Three or more reasons explained:
• Better education for girls means women marry later and choose smaller families
• Greater access to contraception and family planning
• Falling infant mortality means parents need fewer children for some to survive
• Urbanisation reduces the economic value of children (no longer farm labour)
• Growing female employment outside the home delays childbearing
• Government policies (e.g. China's former one-child policy)
Developing: Two reasons given with limited development.
Emerging: One reason or list without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘HDI is a better measure of development than GNI per head.’
Assess this statement.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Sustained argument that weighs HDI's strengths against its weaknesses; includes specific country evidence (UK ≈ 0.93, India ≈ 0.64, Niger ≈ 0.40); reaches a clear and justified conclusion.
Secure (5–6): Both sides argued with examples; some judgement at the end.
Developing (3–4): Lists strengths and weaknesses but limited weighing or evidence.
Emerging (1–2): One-sided answer or general comments.
+3 SPaG.
Indicative content: FOR — HDI captures health and education as well as income, exposes oil-rich states with poor schools, makes inequality between countries clearer; AGAINST — HDI still relies on GNI as one component and on national averages, so it hides regional inequality; data quality varies; it ignores environmental sustainability and human rights. JUDGEMENT — HDI gives a fuller picture than GNI alone, but neither captures everything that matters; both work best alongside other measures. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a physical cause of uneven development?
A) Heavy national debt
B) Colonialism
C) Frequent natural hazards
D) Trade tariffs
practice_questions.marks: C) Frequent natural hazards [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by ‘push factors’ in international migration.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating push factors are reasons that drive people AWAY from a place; 1 mark for naming at least one example (poverty, conflict, drought, unemployment, lack of services). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the impact of remittances on source countries.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Remittances bring money into source-country economies (1 mark)
• They can account for a major share of GDP (e.g. over 30% of GDP in Tajikistan and South Sudan) (1 mark for figure/example)
• Families use the money for food, education and housing, raising quality of life (1 mark)
• They reduce poverty but the country also loses skilled workers (brain drain) (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how historical factors have caused uneven development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear historical causes explained with developed reasoning.
Secure: Two causes explained — e.g. 'Colonial powers extracted raw materials and prevented local industry from developing, so countries inherited weak economies after independence' / 'Borders drawn by colonial rulers ignored ethnic groups, leading to civil wars (e.g. DRC, Sierra Leone) which destroyed infrastructure'.
Developing: Two points named with limited explanation.
Emerging: Lists factors without linking to development.
[4 marks — 2 marks per cause]

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why international migration is a consequence of uneven development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Several developed reasons with examples; clear linkage to development gap.
Secure: Three or more reasons explained:
• Large income gaps create pull from poorer to richer countries (Mexico → USA)
• Wars and instability in poorer regions act as push factors (Syria → Germany)
• Better healthcare and education in HICs attract families (Philippines → UK)
• Family connections already abroad create chain migration
• Climate change and drought make some regions unviable (Sahel)
• Cheap travel and global media spread awareness of opportunities
Developing: Two reasons given with limited examples.
Emerging: One reason or list without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Economic causes are the most important reason for uneven development.’
Assess this statement.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Sustained argument weighing economic causes against physical and historical causes; specific examples (cocoa farmers ~6–10% of bar price; HIPC debt; Haiti earthquake/hurricane; African colonial borders); clear judgement.
Secure (5–6): Both sides argued with examples; some weighing.
Developing (3–4): Lists points but limited weighing or evidence.
Emerging (1–2): One-sided answer or general comments.
+3 SPaG.
Indicative content: FOR economic — primary commodity dependence and unfair trade rules trap countries; debt drains money out of poorer economies; AGAINST — physical factors (landlocked nations, malaria, hazards) handicap countries before any trade; historical colonialism set up the unequal system in the first place. JUDGEMENT — economic causes matter but they are themselves the result of historical colonialism, so the three groups are deeply linked. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of these is the layer with most rainforest species?
A) Emergent layer
B) Canopy
C) Understorey
D) Forest floor
practice_questions.marks: B) Canopy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two physical characteristics of a tropical rainforest.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per characteristic with brief development. Examples: hot temperatures (25–30°C all year); high rainfall (over 2,000 mm/year); no clear seasons; layered structure with emergent, canopy, understorey and floor levels; thin soil but dense vegetation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two adaptations of rainforest plants.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two adaptations described with how they work (e.g. buttress roots spread sideways to support tall trees; drip-tip leaves end in a point so water runs off and prevents mould). Secure: two named with limited explanation. Developing: one adaptation. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain how rainforest plants and climate are interdependent.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — plants release water vapour through transpiration; this forms clouds and rain; the rain supports more plant growth; without trees, transpiration drops and rainfall declines. Secure: identifies transpiration link. Developing: 'plants need rain' alone. Emerging: 'they help each other'.

practice_questions.text: Suggest why biodiversity in tropical rainforests is so high.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three reasons explained — warm wet climate enables year-round growth; layered structure creates many micro-habitats; long evolutionary stability; high productivity supports complex food webs; geographical isolation enables speciation. Secure: two reasons with explanation. Developing: lists reasons. Emerging: 'because it's hot' alone.

practice_questions.text: 'Tropical rainforests are too valuable to humanity to allow further deforestation.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging value (medicines, climate regulation, biodiversity, indigenous people) against pressures (development, poverty, food). Reaches a justified judgement — e.g. that the value is real but cannot be enforced from outside without compensating those who depend on the land. Use of named examples (Amazon, Congo). Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of intermediate technology?
A) A wind turbine farm
B) A nuclear power station
C) A hand-drilled village well
D) A high-speed railway
practice_questions.marks: C) A hand-drilled village well [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline how microfinance loans help reduce the development gap.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying microfinance as small loans (often under £100) given to people without access to normal banks; 1 mark for explaining the impact (allows people, especially women, to start small businesses, lifting their family out of poverty). Reference to Grameen Bank or repayment rate over 95% supports full credit. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of tourism in The Gambia’s economy.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for description with figures:
• Tourism contributes around 20% of GDP (1 mark)
• It provides around 42,000 direct jobs (1 mark)
• Visitors come mainly from the UK, Netherlands and Belgium during the dry season (1 mark)
• Around 235,000 tourists per year (pre-pandemic) (1 mark)
• Concentrated at Atlantic coast resorts like Kotu, Kololi and Senegambia (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how fair trade can reduce inequalities for farmers in low-income countries.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly explained mechanisms with developed reasoning.
Secure: Two ways explained — e.g. 'Fair trade guarantees farmers a minimum price for crops like coffee and cocoa, so income is stable even when world prices fall' / 'A community premium is paid on top of the minimum price, which is spent on local schools and clean water'.
Developing: Two points named with limited explanation.
Emerging: Lists features of fair trade without linking to inequality.
[4 marks — 2 marks per point]

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why tourism in The Gambia has been able to reduce the development gap.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Several developed reasons with named figures and clear linkage to development.
Secure: Three or more reasons explained:
• Warm dry season from November–April attracts winter visitors from northern Europe
• Sandy Atlantic beaches and short flight time from the UK
• Tourism creates ~42,000 direct jobs in hotels and transport
• Multiplier effect: tourist spending circulates through local food, transport and craft sectors
• Tourism levy funds schools and clinics
• Improved airport and roads benefit local people too
• Roots Festival attracts diaspora visitors and builds cultural pride
Developing: Two reasons given with limited evidence.
Emerging: One reason or list without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Tourism is the best strategy for reducing the development gap.’
Assess this statement using a named example.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Sustained argument weighing tourism in The Gambia against other strategies (aid, fair trade, microfinance, debt relief, investment); specific figures (20% GDP, 42,000 jobs, ~60% economic leakage); clear judgement.
Secure (5–6): Both sides argued with examples; some weighing.
Developing (3–4): Lists strengths and weaknesses but limited evidence.
Emerging (1–2): One-sided answer or general comments.
+3 SPaG.
Indicative content: FOR — tourism brought ~20% of Gambian GDP and ~42,000 jobs; multiplier effect, infrastructure spillover, foreign currency. AGAINST — up to 60% economic leakage to overseas firms, seasonal jobs, collapsed during COVID-19; fair trade and microfinance build skills more durably; debt relief frees long-term spending on health and education. JUDGEMENT — tourism is powerful in countries with the right climate and beaches but is fragile, so it works best when combined with other strategies, not on its own. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which is the biggest single cause of Amazon deforestation?
A) Cattle ranching
B) Logging
C) Mining
D) Hydroelectric dams
practice_questions.marks: A) Cattle ranching [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two economic impacts of Amazon deforestation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per impact with development. Examples: beef and soya exports earn billions of dollars; jobs are created in farming and logging; soil erosion damages future farming potential; long-term costs of climate change.

practice_questions.text: Describe the main causes of deforestation in the Amazon.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three causes described with detail (e.g. cattle ranching takes about 80% of cleared land; soya farming for animal feed; legal and illegal logging of hardwoods; mining at Carajás; Trans-Amazonian Highway). Secure: two causes. Developing: one cause. Emerging: vague reference to 'cutting trees'.

practice_questions.text: Explain how deforestation contributes to climate change.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — trees normally absorb CO₂; cutting and burning them releases the stored carbon; less forest means less future absorption; deforestation accounts for around 10% of global emissions. Secure: identifies CO₂ release. Developing: 'cutting trees is bad'. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Compare selective logging and ecotourism as sustainable management strategies.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three contrasts — aim (still extracting timber vs no extraction), income type (timber sales vs visitor fees), scale (working forest vs preserved areas), risk (some forest still lost vs preserved). Comparative connectives. Secure: two contrasts. Developing: lists separately. Emerging: only describes one.

practice_questions.text: 'International action is the most effective way to reduce Amazon deforestation.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument weighing international tools (debt-for-nature swaps, CITES, carbon credits, FSC certification) against local action (selective logging, ecotourism, indigenous land rights, Brazilian government enforcement via DETER). Reaches a justified judgement, e.g. that international action provides funds and frameworks but local enforcement decides outcomes. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes Nigeria's classification as an economy?
A) High-income country (HIC)
B) Newly emerging economy (NEE)
C) Low-income country (LIC)
D) Post-industrial economy
practice_questions.marks: B) Newly emerging economy (NEE) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the location of Nigeria within Africa.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating Nigeria is in West Africa / on the Gulf of Guinea / Atlantic coast; 1 mark for naming at least one bordering country (Benin, Niger, Chad or Cameroon) or noting that it lies entirely within the tropics. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the social and cultural diversity of Nigeria.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Over 250 ethnic groups and 500 languages (1 mark)
• Three dominant groups: Hausa-Fulani (north), Yoruba (south-west), Igbo (south-east) (1 mark for any two)
• Roughly 53% Muslim (mainly north) and 45% Christian (mainly south) (1 mark)
• Globally exported culture: Nollywood (~2,500 films/year), Afrobeats artists (1 mark)
[3 marks — credit accurate, specific points]

practice_questions.text: Explain how Nigeria's environmental context can both help and hinder its development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two well-developed contrasting points with examples.
Secure: Two points clearly explained — e.g. 'Oil reserves in the Niger Delta have generated huge export income, making Nigeria one of the top ten oil producers' (helps) / 'Spills and gas flaring in the Delta have polluted fisheries and farmland, harming local communities' (hinders); 'Fertile southern farmland supports agriculture' (helps) / 'Sahel droughts and southern flooding push farmers off their land' (hinders).
Developing: Points named without development.
Emerging: One side only.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why Nigeria is regionally and globally important.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Several developed reasons with named figures and balanced regional + global view.
Secure: Three or more reasons explained:
• Largest economy in Africa for most of the last decade
• Most populous African country (~225 million); will pass USA before 2050
• Africa's biggest oil producer; over 80% of exports come from oil and gas
• Founder member of ECOWAS and the African Union, and an OPEC member; diplomatic leadership in West Africa
• Cultural reach: Nollywood films and Afrobeats music exported worldwide
• Major ports at Lagos and Port Harcourt link West Africa to Europe and Asia
Developing: Two reasons given with limited evidence.
Emerging: One reason or list without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Political stability is the most important factor in Nigeria's recent economic growth.’
Assess this statement.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Sustained argument weighing political stability against economic, social and environmental factors; specific examples (1999 return to democracy; 5–7% GDP growth 2000–14; 2015 and 2023 peaceful handovers; corruption rank 25/100; Boko Haram in north-east); clear judgement.
Secure (5–6): Both sides argued with examples; some weighing.
Developing (3–4): Lists points without weighing or evidence.
Emerging (1–2): One-sided answer.
+3 SPaG.
Indicative content: FOR — democratic elections since 1999 boosted foreign investment; peaceful handovers in 2015 and 2023 strengthened confidence; AGAINST — high oil prices drove growth more than politics; young population and diversification into telecoms/banking/Nollywood matter; Boko Haram and corruption persist despite democracy. JUDGEMENT — political stability is necessary but not sufficient: Nigeria has grown when democracy AND oil prices AND a young workforce align. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Hot deserts typically receive how much rainfall a year?
A) Less than 250 mm
B) Around 500 mm
C) Around 1,000 mm
D) Over 2,000 mm
practice_questions.marks: A) Less than 250 mm [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two adaptations of plants to hot deserts.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per adaptation with development. Examples: thick fleshy stems store water (cacti); waxy skins reduce evaporation; spines instead of leaves cut water loss; deep roots reach the water table; wide shallow roots collect rare rainfall.

practice_questions.text: Describe two physical characteristics of a hot desert.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two characteristics described with figures (rainfall under 250 mm/year; daytime temperatures over 45°C; large diurnal range with cold nights; sparse vegetation; sandy or rocky landscape). Secure: two named with limited detail. Developing: vague. Emerging: 'they're hot'.

practice_questions.text: Explain how camels are adapted to live in hot deserts.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — humps store fat (broken down to release water); large feet spread weight on sand; double eyelashes block dust; can drink 100 litres in minutes; tolerate 25% body water loss. At least three adaptations with mechanism. Secure: two adaptations named with explanation. Developing: lists features. Emerging: 'they're suited'.

practice_questions.text: Compare two challenges of developing hot desert environments.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three contrasts — e.g. extreme heat (working hours limited) vs water supply (long-term sustainability), or inaccessibility (huge initial investment) vs water (ongoing constraint). Comparative connectives. Use of named place. Secure: two contrasts. Developing: lists. Emerging: only one challenge.

practice_questions.text: 'The economic opportunities of hot deserts outweigh the challenges of developing them.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named opportunities (Pilbara mining, solar farms, Uluru tourism) and challenges (heat, water, inaccessibility, indigenous land conflict). Reaches a justified judgement, e.g. that opportunities can outweigh challenges only when paired with sustainable water use and respect for indigenous land. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a transnational corporation operating in Nigeria?
A) A family-run market stall in Lagos
B) Shell
C) The Federal Ministry of Industry
D) A farmers' co-operative in Kano
practice_questions.marks: B) Shell [1 mark — Shell is a TNC headquartered in the UK / Netherlands with major operations in Nigeria]

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by a transnational corporation (TNC).
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating a TNC is a company with operations in more than one country; 1 mark for naming an example operating in Nigeria (Shell, ExxonMobil, MTN, Unilever, Cadbury, Chevron, TotalEnergies). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how Nigeria's industrial structure has changed since independence.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Share of agriculture in GDP has fallen sharply (from ~70% of workers in 1960 to ~22% of GDP today) (1 mark)
• Manufacturing / industry has grown to around 25% of GDP (1 mark)
• Services now make up the largest share at around 53% of GDP (1 mark)
• Examples of new industries: cement (Dangote), food/drinks, vehicles, telecoms, pharmaceuticals (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of manufacturing has stimulated economic growth in Nigeria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear mechanisms with developed examples.
Secure: Two ways explained — e.g. 'Manufacturing adds value to raw materials: turning cocoa into chocolate or limestone into Dangote cement earns far more than exporting raw goods, increasing GDP' / 'New factories create skilled jobs and pay taxes; the multiplier effect creates more jobs in transport, food and suppliers, raising regional incomes'.
Developing: Two points named with limited explanation.
Emerging: Lists facts without linking to growth.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest both advantages and disadvantages of transnational corporations (TNCs) for Nigeria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Several developed advantages AND disadvantages with named TNCs and balanced view.
Secure: At least three points across both sides:
Advantages:
• Foreign investment Nigeria could not provide (Shell ~6,000 direct jobs)
• Skills transfer to local engineers/managers
• Telecoms TNCs (e.g. MTN) extended mobile and mobile-banking to 200m+ Nigerians
• Tax revenue and infrastructure (schools, clinics)
Disadvantages:
• Profits leave for TNC headquarters abroad
• Oil spills in Niger Delta have killed fisheries
• Tax avoidance through transfer pricing
• Decisions made overseas, vulnerable to relocation
Developing: Two points given but unbalanced or without examples.
Emerging: One side only.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Changing trade links with China and India have been more important for Nigeria's economy than its TNCs.’
Assess this statement.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Sustained argument weighing changing trade links against TNCs' role; specific examples (China = largest source of imports; India = biggest crude buyer; Lagos–Ibadan railway funded by China; AfCFTA from 2021; Shell ~6,000 jobs and Niger Delta pollution; MTN telecoms reach); clear judgement.
Secure (5–6): Both sides argued with examples; some weighing.
Developing (3–4): Lists points without weighing or evidence.
Emerging (1–2): One-sided answer.
+3 SPaG.
Indicative content: FOR — China-funded infrastructure (Lagos–Ibadan rail) supports the whole economy; India buys most oil so sets the price Nigeria receives; AfCFTA opens new African markets. AGAINST — TNCs employ tens of thousands directly, transferred mobile-phone technology to 200m+ Nigerians, and their tax revenues fund the federal budget; without TNCs the export oil industry would not exist in the first place. JUDGEMENT — both reinforce each other: TNCs produce the goods and oil that flow through the new trade routes, so neither alone explains growth. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
What is desertification?
A) When sand dunes spread
B) When fertile land turns into desert
C) When deserts shrink
D) When deserts get more rainfall
practice_questions.marks: B) When fertile land turns into desert [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two human causes of desertification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per cause with development. Examples: removal of fuelwood (trees felled for cooking, soil exposed); overgrazing (too many livestock strip vegetation); over-cultivation (continuous farming exhausts soil); population growth (increases pressure on land).

practice_questions.text: Describe two strategies used to reduce desertification.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two strategies with detail (e.g. magic stones along contours trap rainwater; tree planting under the Great Green Wall binds soil and provides shade). Secure: two strategies named. Developing: one strategy. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why climate change makes desertification worse.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — rising temperatures increase evaporation; rainfall is becoming less reliable in semi-arid zones; longer droughts kill vegetation; without vegetation, soil erodes; less land is productive; pressure on the remaining land grows. Secure: identifies climate change effect on rainfall/evaporation. Developing: 'climate change is bad'. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Suggest why the Great Green Wall has progressed more slowly than originally planned.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three reasons explained — wrong species in early plantings died; conflict in Mali/Burkina Faso/Niger blocked access; funding shortfalls from donors; project depends on local farmer engagement, not just outside planting. Secure: two reasons. Developing: one. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: 'The most effective way to reduce desertification is local action by farmers, not large international projects.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with examples on both sides — local actions (mulching, magic stones, fuel-efficient stoves) work small-scale and cheaply; large international projects (Great Green Wall) provide funding, framework and political will but face delivery challenges. Reaches a justified judgement that both are needed; international resources are wasted without local engagement, but local action alone cannot match the scale of climate change. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a destructive wave?
A) Low and long with strong swash
B) Tall and steep with strong backwash
C) Slow and gentle with no backwash
D) Always found in summer only
practice_questions.marks: B) Tall and steep with strong backwash [1 mark]
