practice_questions.text: Outline two ways waves transport sediment along the coast.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per process named with brief development. Examples: longshore drift — zigzag movement caused by waves arriving at an angle and backwash returning straight down; suspension — fine sediment carried in the water column; traction — large pebbles rolled along the seabed; saltation — small pebbles bouncing along the seabed; solution — dissolved minerals carried in seawater.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between mechanical and chemical weathering at the coast.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear contrast with named example of each — mechanical (e.g. freeze–thaw on chalk South Downs cliffs, water freezes and expands by 9% in cracks) versus chemical (e.g. carbonation, rainwater forms a weak acid that dissolves limestone). Secure: both types defined with one example. Developing: only one type explained. Emerging: terms confused or undefined.

practice_questions.text: Explain how hydraulic power erodes a cliff.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — waves slam into the cliff face; air is trapped and compressed in cracks at high pressure; as the wave retreats the air expands explosively; this widens the cracks and prises rock fragments away. Most powerful during storms on hard-rock coasts. Secure: process explained with mechanism. Developing: defines hydraulic power but no mechanism. Emerging: 'waves break the rock' alone.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why longshore drift moves sediment further on Atlantic-facing UK coasts than on sheltered North Sea coasts.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three factors compared — longer fetch on Atlantic coast (thousands of kilometres) generates larger, higher-energy waves; prevailing south-westerly winds drive consistent angled approach; greater wave energy carries larger sediment further; in contrast the North Sea has shorter fetch, more variable wind direction and lower wave energy. References named coasts (e.g. Cornwall, Pembrokeshire vs East Yorkshire). Secure: two factors with comparison. Developing: lists differences without comparative connectives. Emerging: factors confused or unconnected.

practice_questions.text: 'Wave processes are more important than weathering and mass movement in shaping the UK coast.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with specific UK examples and a justified judgement. For: hydraulic power and abrasion shape almost all hard-rock cliffs; longshore drift constantly redistributes sediment; storm waves cause the most visible change. Against: on soft-rock coasts like Holderness, slumping (mass movement) does most of the work; freeze–thaw and carbonation prepare the rock long before waves can erode it; without prior weathering, hydraulic power has fewer cracks to attack. Reaches a judgement that the answer depends on geology — wave processes dominate hard-rock coasts, mass movement and weathering dominate soft-rock coasts. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists processes without judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of bottom-up aid in Nigeria?
A) The Lagos urban water network funded by the World Bank
B) UN food aid following the 2022 floods
C) An NGO training village women in improved farming techniques
D) Chinese loans to fund the Lagos–Ibadan railway
practice_questions.marks: C) An NGO training village women in improved farming techniques [1 mark — bottom-up aid is small, community-led]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between short-term and long-term aid.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining short-term aid is emergency response after disasters (e.g. food and clean water after the 2022 floods); 1 mark for explaining long-term aid funds infrastructure, health or education over years (e.g. UK FCDO investment in Nigerian schools and clinics). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the environmental impacts of oil extraction in the Niger Delta.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Oil spills from pipelines — over 13 million barrels leaked since the 1970s (1 mark)
• Loss of fisheries and contamination of farmland on which ~60% of Delta residents rely (1 mark)
• Gas flaring releases CO₂ and toxic particulates, contributing to climate change (1 mark)
• Mangrove forests destroyed by oil contamination, affecting biodiversity (1 mark)
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how aid has improved quality of life in Nigeria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clear ways with developed examples and figures.
Secure: Two ways explained — e.g. 'World Health Organization, UNICEF and Gates Foundation vaccination programmes eliminated polio in Nigeria in 2020, ending lifelong disabilities for thousands of children' / 'NGO training of women farmers raises rural incomes through better crops, lifting whole families out of food insecurity'. Reference to under-5 mortality falling from 200 to ~110 per 1,000 strengthens marks.
Developing: Two points named with limited explanation.
Emerging: Lists aid types without linking to quality of life.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why economic development has not improved quality of life equally across Nigeria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Several developed reasons covering political, economic and environmental factors.
Secure: Three or more reasons explained:
• North-south divide: Lagos has ~4% poverty, Sokoto over 80%
• Boko Haram has destroyed schools and clinics in the north-east
• Niger Delta oil communities bear pollution but receive little wealth
• Most TNC profits leave for headquarters abroad
• Rural areas lack reliable power and clean water
• Corruption diverts public spending from poorer regions
• Climate change makes Sahel drought and southern flooding worse, hitting farmers hardest
Developing: Two reasons given with limited evidence.
Emerging: One reason or list without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The environmental cost of Nigeria's development is too high.’
Assess this statement.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Sustained argument weighing environmental damage against the development benefits; specific evidence (13 million barrels of oil spilled, 350,000 hectares lost to desertification a year, polio eliminated 2020, life expectancy 47→55, ~40% poverty); clear judgement.
Secure (5–6): Both sides argued with examples; some weighing.
Developing (3–4): Lists points without weighing or evidence.
Emerging (1–2): One-sided answer.
+3 SPaG.
Indicative content: FOR — Niger Delta oil spills have destroyed fisheries that 60% of Delta residents depend on; gas flaring contributes to climate change; northern desertification displaces farmers; Lagos air and water pollution harms health. AGAINST — life expectancy has risen by 8 years, under-5 mortality has nearly halved, polio eliminated, tens of millions lifted from extreme poverty. JUDGEMENT — for the Niger Delta and northern Sahel the cost has been too high; for the country as a whole the gains are real but cleaner growth is needed. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a depositional coastal landform?
A) Wave-cut platform
B) Stack
C) Spit
D) Cave
practice_questions.marks: C) Spit [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between a discordant and a concordant coastline.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct contrast. Discordant: rock layers run at right angles to the sea, producing alternating hard headlands and soft bays (e.g. Swanage). Concordant: rock layers run parallel to the sea, producing long straight cliffs broken only where the sea breaks through (e.g. Lulworth Cove area).

practice_questions.text: Describe the formation of a wave-cut platform.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear three-stage sequence — waves attack the base of the cliff (hydraulic power, abrasion); a wave-cut notch forms; the cliff above is undermined and collapses; the cliff retreats, leaving a flat rocky surface (the platform) exposed at low tide. Names a UK example (Hunstanton, Robin Hood's Bay). Secure: two stages with mechanism. Developing: vague reference to erosion. Emerging: missing the notch or collapse.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a stack forms from a headland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — cracks in the headland are widened by hydraulic power and abrasion; a cave forms at the base; continued erosion forms an arch through the headland; the roof of the arch eventually collapses, leaving a stack standing offshore. Named example: Old Harry Rocks (Dorset). Secure: most stages with mechanism. Developing: stages out of order or missing one. Emerging: terms used without sequence.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why Spurn Head has formed where it has.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three linked reasons — longshore drift moves sediment southwards along the Holderness coast (around 1.5 m per day) from soft boulder-clay cliffs further north; at the Humber Estuary the coast changes direction, but the sediment keeps moving in its original direction; the Humber's calm sheltered water lets the sediment settle and build out as a spit; recurved end shaped by occasional waves from a different direction during storms; salt marsh has developed in the sheltered water behind. Named locations and figures throughout. Secure: two factors with explanation. Developing: lists features. Emerging: vague references.

practice_questions.text: 'Geology is more important than wave processes in shaping the UK coast.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named UK examples and a justified judgement. For: Dorset's headlands and bays only exist because hard chalk meets soft clay; Holderness retreats fastest where boulder clay is exposed; Lulworth Cove formed because the sea broke through harder rock to softer rock behind. Against: even hard rock erodes given enough wave energy; storm waves and hydraulic power are responsible for the actual cutting; longshore drift, not geology, builds Spurn Head. Reaches a judgement that geology controls where landforms form, but wave processes control how fast. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists features without judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes deindustrialisation?
A) The growth of manufacturing industries
B) The decline of traditional manufacturing industries and loss of jobs
C) The closure of all primary sector employment
D) The shift from tertiary to secondary sector employment
practice_questions.marks: B) The decline of traditional manufacturing industries and loss of jobs [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two causes of deindustrialisation in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per cause identified with brief development. Examples: cheaper foreign competition (lower wages overseas undercut UK manufacturers); outdated machinery (lower productivity than rivals); resource exhaustion (UK coal seams running out); government policy (privatisation and reduced subsidies in the 1980s); higher UK labour costs.

practice_questions.text: Describe the change in UK manufacturing employment since 1970.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear pattern with quantification (e.g. ‘manufacturing employment fell from around 7 million in 1970 to about 2.5 million today, a drop of more than half’) and reference to a region or industry. Secure: clear decline trend with one figure. Developing: states that manufacturing fell without figures or named regions. Emerging: vague claim that ‘jobs were lost’.

practice_questions.text: Explain how globalisation has changed the UK economy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — cheaper imports forced UK manufacturers to close, AND UK service industries (finance, education, creative) expanded into a global market, supported by container shipping and digital communication. Includes a TNC example such as Nissan or Tata. Secure: identifies one positive and one negative effect with explanation. Developing: lists effects without explaining the mechanism. Emerging: states globalisation happened without saying how it changed the UK.

practice_questions.text: Compare the primary and tertiary sectors in the UK economy today.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three points of comparison using comparative connectives (whereas, in contrast, while), supported by examples — e.g. employment share (primary under 2% vs tertiary over 80%), location (primary scattered, tertiary clustered in cities and London), value (primary lower output, tertiary dominant). Secure: two clear comparisons with examples. Developing: lists features of each sector separately without comparison. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that government policy was the main cause of deindustrialisation in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the role of 1980s privatisation and reduced subsidies in speeding up coal and steel closures, while evaluating the deeper drivers — cheaper foreign competition, outdated machinery, resource exhaustion — that would have caused decline regardless. Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. ‘policy accelerated decline that global market forces had already made inevitable’). Secure: two-sided argument with one or two factors weighed against policy. Developing: lists factors with limited evaluation or judgement. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines a science park?
A) A nature reserve protected by the government
B) A theme park about science
C) A planned cluster of research-led firms, often near a university
D) A government laboratory closed to the public
practice_questions.marks: C) A planned cluster of research-led firms, often near a university [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why rural areas may experience population growth.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: good commuter access to nearby cities (workers can live rural and travel in); higher quality of life (cheaper housing than the city, more space, less traffic); remote/home working makes physical office attendance unnecessary; better local schools attract families.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location of UK science parks.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies clustering near research universities (e.g. Cambridge Science Park linked to Trinity College, Manchester near the university), often with motorway/rail access, and notes that they are concentrated in the south and east. Secure: clear pattern with one named example. Developing: vague claim about ‘cities’ without naming. Emerging: states that science parks ‘exist in the UK’.

practice_questions.text: Explain how modern industrial development can be more environmentally sustainable.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: develops a specific example (e.g. Nissan Sunderland) and links its features (on-site wind turbines, rainwater capture, paint solvent recycling) to reduced carbon emissions and lower water use. Secure: identifies one green feature with explanation of its effect. Developing: states that modern factories are ‘cleaner’ without naming features. Emerging: vague claim about ‘eco-friendly industry’.

practice_questions.text: Compare a UK rural area of population growth with one of population decline.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: names both areas (e.g. South Cambridgeshire vs Outer Hebrides) and uses three comparative points covering jobs, accessibility and services. Uses comparative language. Secure: names both and gives two contrasts with examples. Developing: describes each separately without comparison. Emerging: only one area named.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that science and business parks are the most important driver of the UK’s post-industrial economy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the role of science parks (Cambridge Science Park clusters research, attracts investment, creates skilled jobs) but evaluating that financial services, ICT and the NHS employ far more people than science parks alone, and London-based services dominate UK economic output. Reaches a justified judgement. Secure: two-sided argument with one or two factors weighed against science parks. Developing: lists factors with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a soft engineering strategy?
A) Sea wall
B) Rock armour
C) Beach nourishment
D) Gabions
practice_questions.marks: C) Beach nourishment [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why the Holderness coast erodes so quickly.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per linked reason. Examples: weak boulder-clay cliffs (no cement holding the rock together, slumps when saturated); long North Sea fetch and exposure to destructive easterly storm waves; shallow offshore zone keeps wave energy high at the cliff base; longshore drift carries away fallen material exposing the cliff to fresh attack.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by managed retreat.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear definition with mechanism and example — defences are removed or not built; the sea is allowed to advance to a new line further inland; compensation is paid to landowners; salt marsh and mudflats re-establish as a natural buffer (e.g. used on parts of Holderness for low-value farmland). Secure: definition with one feature. Developing: vague reference to letting the sea in. Emerging: terms confused.

practice_questions.text: Explain how groynes at Mappleton have caused increased erosion at Cowden.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — longshore drift carries sediment southwards along the Holderness coast at 1.5 m per day; the Mappleton groynes (built 1991) trap that sediment to build up Mappleton's beach; less sediment then reaches Cowden, 3 km south; without a beach to absorb wave energy, Cowden's cliffs are exposed to direct wave attack and erode faster. Secure: most stages with mechanism. Developing: links the two but no figures. Emerging: 'walls cause erosion' alone.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why some sections of the Holderness coast are defended while others are allowed to retreat.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three reasons compared — high-value places (Bridlington, Hornsea, Withernsea, Easington Gas Terminal which processes 25% of UK gas) justify the cost of hard engineering; defending all 61 km would cost £370 million and far exceed the value of farmland; defences in one place worsen erosion further along the coast (Mappleton-Cowden); managed retreat allows sediment to keep supplying Spurn Head and protect the Humber. Secure: two reasons with comparison. Developing: lists reasons without comparing. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: 'Hard engineering causes more problems than it solves on the Holderness coast.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples and a justified judgement. For: groynes at Mappleton starved Cowden of sediment, accelerating erosion; sea walls reflect wave energy and scour the beach in front; gabions are ugly and short-lived; defending one place deflects erosion onto the next. Against: Mappleton's 500 m sea wall (£2 million in 1991) saved the village; Easington Gas Terminal is defended because it processes 25% of the UK gas supply; without hard engineering whole communities would be lost. Reaches a judgement that hard engineering is worth it for high-value places but creates conflict at the boundaries with undefended sections. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists strategies.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following processes dominates in the upper course of a river?
A) Lateral erosion
B) Vertical erosion
C) Deposition
D) Solution
practice_questions.marks: B) Vertical erosion [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways a river transports its load.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per process named with brief development. Examples: traction (boulders rolled along the bed); saltation (small pebbles bouncing along in hops); suspension (fine sand and silt held up in the water column); solution (dissolved minerals carried invisibly).

practice_questions.text: Describe the cross profile of a river in its upper course.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear three-feature description — narrow channel, steep V-shaped valley, rough bed of angular boulders, interlocking spurs jutting from alternate sides; vertical erosion dominates because the river is cutting down towards sea level. Secure: two features with reasons. Developing: V-shape stated without development. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain how attrition reduces the size of pebbles in a river.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full mechanism — pebbles already in the river collide with each other as they are carried; small fragments break off; the pebbles become progressively smaller, smoother and rounder; over time this is why upper-course rivers carry angular boulders while lower-course rivers carry rounded pebbles. Notes that attrition shapes the load rather than the channel. Secure: clear explanation with mechanism. Developing: definition only. Emerging: confuses with abrasion.

practice_questions.text: Compare the dominant processes in the upper and lower courses of a river.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three points using comparative connectives — upper course is dominated by vertical erosion (cutting down) whereas lower course is dominated by lateral erosion and deposition; the upper course has high energy relative to its load (carrying angular boulders short distances) whereas the lower course has lower energy but higher discharge (carrying fine silt long distances); the upper course channel is rough so energy is lost to friction whereas the lower course is smooth so the river flows efficiently. Secure: two compared points. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: 'A river uses its energy more efficiently in the lower course than in the upper course.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with a justified judgement. For: lower course channels are smoother and wider so less energy is lost to friction; the river can carry a much larger load with a tiny gradient; discharge is highest here, transporting silt and clay long distances. Against: the upper course needs more energy to overcome friction with rough boulders, but it does succeed in cutting deep V-shaped valleys; without the upper-course erosion there would be no load to transport downstream. Reaches a judgement that 'efficient' depends on what you measure — the lower course is efficient at moving large volumes; the upper course is efficient at vertical cutting given low discharge. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists features.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the UK’s north–south divide?
A) A physical mountain range
B) An economic and social gap between the south-east and the north and west
C) The border between England and Scotland
D) A line drawn for political reasons only
practice_questions.marks: B) An economic and social gap between the south-east and the north and west [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons for the UK’s north–south divide.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: deindustrialisation hit the north, Midlands and Wales hardest; new high-tech and finance jobs cluster in London and the south-east; transport links between London and the south-east are stronger than those across the north; London is the political and financial capital, attracting head offices.

practice_questions.text: Describe the UK’s trading links with the wider world.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies the EU as the largest combined trade partner, the US as the largest single-country market, and names other significant partners (China, India). Notes a roughly £700 billion total. Secure: identifies two named partners with one figure. Developing: states the UK trades globally without naming partners. Emerging: vague reference to ‘exports’.

practice_questions.text: Explain how transport investment can reduce the north–south divide.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — faster east-west rail (Trans-Pennine Route Upgrade) cuts journey times between northern cities, attracting business investment, lifting wages and reducing the gap with London. Specific examples used. Secure: identifies one project and explains its effect. Developing: lists projects without explaining mechanism. Emerging: states transport ‘helps the north’ without detail.

practice_questions.text: Compare the role of the European Union with the role of the Commonwealth in the UK’s global links.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three points of comparison — trade volume (EU largest, Commonwealth smaller), geography (EU close, Commonwealth global), nature (EU economic and regulatory, Commonwealth cultural and political). Comparative connectives used. Secure: two clear comparisons with examples. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: only one feature named.

practice_questions.text: Assess the success of UK government strategies in reducing the north–south divide.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging successes (Northern Powerhouse and devolution have raised investment in Greater Manchester, transport upgrades like the Elizabeth Line and Trans-Pennine route improve connectivity, enterprise zones brought firms to Tees Valley) but evaluating limits (London still attracts disproportionate investment, HS2 northern sections cut, life-expectancy gaps remain). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. ‘progress is real but slow, and the gap remains’). Secure: two-sided argument with one or two factors weighed. Developing: lists strategies with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines food miles?
A) The distance a runner travels for food
B) The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
C) The number of food shops in a city
D) The size of an average UK farm
practice_questions.marks: B) The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons UK food self-sufficiency has fallen.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: rising demand for year-round seasonal produce (strawberries in December); cheap imports from countries with lower production costs; consumer demand for variety beyond UK climate range; loss of UK farmland to housing; greater demand for ready meals using imported ingredients.

practice_questions.text: Describe the UK’s pattern of water surplus and deficit.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear north-and-west surplus (over 2,000 mm rainfall in western Scotland and the Lake District) versus south-and-east deficit (under 700 mm in London, East Anglia, East Midlands), with named places. Secure: identifies the surplus and deficit pattern with one named place. Developing: vague claim about ‘more water in the north’. Emerging: states the UK has water without describing pattern.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the UK’s energy mix has changed since 1990.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: develops at least two changes with explanation — coal fell from around 67% to under 1% as climate policy and renewable costs shifted; renewables rose to over 40% with North Sea offshore wind (Hornsea); gas remains important; nuclear capacity is being rebuilt at Hinkley Point C. Secure: one detailed change with explanation. Developing: notes change without explanation. Emerging: vague reference to ‘greener energy’.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why the UK relies on water transfer schemes such as Kielder Water and the Elan Valley.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed reasons — uneven rainfall (north and west wet, south and east dry), uneven population (concentrated in dry areas), high urban water demand for homes and industry, ageing systems needing reservoir support, climate change increasing summer drought risk. Names schemes (Kielder Water in Northumberland, Elan Valley supplying Birmingham). Secure: two clear reasons with examples. Developing: lists reasons without development. Emerging: only one reason, no example.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that imports are now the biggest threat to UK resource security.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the scale of imports (food self-sufficiency falling, gas and oil increasingly imported, electricity interconnectors with France and Norway) but evaluating other threats (climate change altering rainfall patterns, ageing nuclear stations, rising domestic demand, biodiversity loss in farmland). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. ‘imports raise vulnerability, but climate change is a deeper structural threat’). Secure: two-sided argument with one or two factors weighed. Developing: lists threats with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following landforms is most associated with the upper course of a river?
A) Estuary
B) Levee
C) Waterfall
D) Ox-bow lake
practice_questions.marks: C) Waterfall [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between a river cliff and a slip-off slope.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct contrast. River cliff: a steep eroded bank on the outer bend of a meander, where water flow is fastest and lateral erosion deepens the channel. Slip-off slope: a gentle bank of deposited sand and shingle on the inner bend, where water flow is slowest.

practice_questions.text: Describe the formation of interlocking spurs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear three-feature description — in the upper course the river has limited energy and cannot cut sideways through hills; vertical erosion dominates so the river weaves between obstacles; the result is ridges projecting from alternate sides of the V-shaped valley around which the river bends. Secure: two features explained. Developing: identifies the shape only. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a waterfall and gorge form.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — a band of hard rock lies over softer rock; the soft rock is eroded faster, leaving the hard rock as an overhang; the river plunges over the step, eroding a deep plunge pool by hydraulic action and abrasion; the plunge pool undercuts the hard rock which eventually collapses; the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a steep narrow gorge. UK example named (High Force). Secure: most stages with mechanism. Developing: stages out of order. Emerging: identifies waterfall but no process.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why ox-bow lakes are more common in the lower course than in the upper course of a river.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three linked reasons — ox-bow lakes form from meanders, which only develop where lateral erosion dominates (the lower middle and lower courses); the upper course is dominated by vertical erosion in narrow V-valleys, so meanders cannot form; the lower course has a wide flat flood plain and gentle gradient that allow the river to swing freely; flood discharge is highest near the mouth, providing the energy needed to cut across a meander neck. Secure: two reasons compared. Developing: lists features. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: 'A river's lower-course landforms are shaped more by deposition than by erosion.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples and a justified judgement. For: levees and flood plains are built by repeated deposition during floods; estuaries develop wide mudflats from deposited silt; the lower Severn's ox-bow lakes are sealed off by deposition. Against: ox-bow lakes only form because lateral erosion first cuts a meander; the wide flat valley is itself the result of long-term lateral erosion; even at the mouth, hydraulic action erodes the channel during floods. Reaches a judgement that lower-course landforms are mostly built by deposition, but the wider valley shape that allows them to exist is the product of long-term erosion. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists features.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best defines an energy deficit country?
A) A country that produces more energy than it consumes
B) A country that produces less energy than it consumes
C) A country with no electricity grid
D) A country with only renewable energy
practice_questions.marks: B) A country that produces less energy than it consumes [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why global energy demand is rising.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: economic development (industrialising countries use more power); population growth (more people to supply, world reached 8 billion in 2022); rising use of technology (electric vehicles, data centres, air conditioning); higher living standards (more home appliances).

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of oil reserves.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies the Middle East as holding around 50% of known oil reserves, with significant reserves in Russia, the United States and Venezuela, and notes that consumption is concentrated in different regions (North America, Europe, East Asia). Secure: names the Middle East and one other region. Developing: vague reference to ‘a few countries’. Emerging: states ‘oil exists worldwide’.

practice_questions.text: Explain how political factors can affect energy supply.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — sanctions, conflicts and trade alliances change which suppliers can sell, raising prices and forcing buyers to switch sources. Specific example such as the 2022 invasion of Ukraine cutting Russian gas to Europe and pushing wholesale prices up by over five times. Secure: identifies one political factor with example. Developing: states politics ‘changes prices’ without example. Emerging: vague claim about politics.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why energy insecurity can damage food production.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed reasons — modern farming depends on fertiliser (made from natural gas), irrigation pumps need electricity, refrigeration relies on continuous power, transport of food uses oil-derived fuels, and rising fuel costs feed straight through to higher food prices (UK 2022–23 example). Secure: two clear reasons with examples. Developing: lists reasons without development. Emerging: only one reason.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that political factors are now the most important influence on global energy supply.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the power of political events (Russia–Ukraine 2022, OPEC oil decisions, sanctions on Iran and Venezuela) against other influences (physical reserves limit options, technology unlocked shale gas and offshore wind, cost of exploitation decides whether reserves are usable). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. ‘politics can dominate in the short term, but physical and technology factors set the long-term picture’). Secure: two-sided argument with one or two factors weighed. Developing: lists factors with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes lag time on a storm hydrograph?
A) The total amount of rain that fell during the storm
B) The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge
C) The maximum discharge of the river
D) The depth of water in the channel
practice_questions.marks: B) The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two physical factors that increase the flood risk of a drainage basin.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per factor named with brief development. Examples: heavy or prolonged precipitation overwhelms the channel; impermeable rock (granite, clay) stops infiltration so water runs off; steep relief shortens lag time; saturated soil after previous rain cannot absorb more; snowmelt during a sudden thaw.

practice_questions.text: Describe the features of a flashy storm hydrograph.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three features — short lag time between peak rainfall and peak discharge; steep rising limb showing rapid rise in discharge; high peak discharge; steep falling limb showing the river drains quickly. Identifies it as typical of urban or upland basins. Secure: two features identified. Developing: vague reference to 'fast'. Emerging: terms confused.

practice_questions.text: Explain how urbanisation increases the flood risk of a drainage basin.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — concrete, tarmac and roof tiles are impermeable so rainwater cannot infiltrate; rainwater is collected by storm drains and carried to the river much faster than natural flow; the result is a shorter lag time and higher peak discharge; new housing on flood plains also increases the value of property at risk. Secure: most stages with mechanism. Developing: lists urban features. Emerging: 'cities flood' alone.

practice_questions.text: Compare the likely flood response of an upland Cumbrian basin and a chalk Oxfordshire basin to the same heavy storm.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three points using comparative connectives — the Cumbrian basin has steep relief whereas the Oxfordshire basin is gentler; Cumbrian rocks (slate, shale) are impermeable whereas chalk is permeable; the Cumbrian basin therefore has a flashier hydrograph (short lag, steep rising limb, high peak); the chalk basin has a smoother hydrograph (longer lag, gentle limb, lower peak); flood risk is much higher in Cumbria. Secure: two compared points. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: 'Human activity is now more important than physical factors in shaping UK flood risk.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with named examples and a justified judgement. For: urbanisation has dramatically shortened lag times in basins like the lower Thames; deforestation increases runoff; building on flood plains has put 5.2 million UK homes at risk; climate change (caused by human activity) is making rainfall events more intense, with a downpour like Storm Desmond now about 40% more likely than a century ago. Against: physical factors (relief, geology, the simple fact of heavy rainfall) still set the baseline; the Cumbrian basin would flood even with no human presence; without steep relief and impermeable rock, no amount of urbanisation would create a flashy hydrograph. Reaches a judgement that human activity now amplifies the underlying physical risk — the physical factors set the stage, human factors decide the scale of the consequences. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists factors.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a soft engineering strategy?
A) Embankments
B) Channel straightening
C) Flood plain zoning
D) Dams and reservoirs
practice_questions.marks: C) Flood plain zoning [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways a dam and reservoir can manage flood risk.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per linked point. Examples: stores excess water during heavy rainfall to prevent it reaching downstream towns; releases water slowly to keep downstream discharge below flood levels; can also generate hydroelectric power and supply drinking water; protects downstream property from a sudden surge in discharge.

practice_questions.text: Describe one soft engineering strategy used in UK flood management.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear three-feature description — chooses one strategy (e.g. tree planting at Pickering); explains the mechanism (woodland and leaky dams slow runoff and increase lag time); gives a figure (40 hectares planted; flood discharge cut by 15–20%); identifies it as cheaper than hard defences. Secure: two features. Developing: identifies strategy without mechanism. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why upstream tree planting is an effective flood management strategy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — trees absorb rainwater through their roots and slow runoff; their canopy intercepts rain before it hits the ground; the leaf litter on the woodland floor acts like a sponge; together these increase lag time and reduce peak discharge downstream. Cites Pickering 15–20% reduction as evidence. Secure: most stages with mechanism. Developing: identifies trees absorb water without mechanism. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why a UK flood scheme might combine hard and soft engineering rather than using one approach alone.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three linked reasons — soft engineering (tree planting, river restoration) cuts upstream discharge but cannot guarantee protection in extreme events; hard barriers protect specific town centres but only the sections that have them and are expensive at scale; combining them means upstream measures slow the flood while downstream barriers protect property; the Severn scheme uses upstream Welsh tree planting plus demountable Bewdley barriers, so the cheaper soft work reduces how often the more expensive barriers need to be deployed. Secure: two reasons compared. Developing: lists reasons. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: 'The River Severn flood scheme has been successful overall.' Assess this view, referring to social, economic and environmental issues.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument across all three issue types with a justified judgement. For: 70 Bewdley properties protected; £7 damage avoided per £1 spent; warnings issued up to 36 hours ahead save lives and possessions; tree planting supports wildlife and sequesters carbon. Against: some communities (e.g. Beales Corner) still flood and feel abandoned; hard barriers disrupt riparian habitats; demountable barriers need volunteer labour to deploy; total cost £9 million plus ongoing maintenance. Reaches a judgement that the scheme has been a clear success in protected sections but raises difficult questions about which areas are worth defending. Secure: balanced with examples across at least two issue types. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists features.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a non-renewable source of energy?
A) Wind
B) Coal
C) Solar
D) Tidal
practice_questions.marks: B) Coal [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two advantages of renewable energy.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per advantage with brief development. Examples: low carbon emissions help meet climate targets; sources replenish naturally so cannot run out; can be installed at small scale in remote areas; cuts dependence on imports; falling costs make solar and wind affordable.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location of the Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies it as a small community in mountainous northern Peru, in South America, in a region of around 60 farming villages without grid electricity. Secure: identifies Peru and the rural mountainous setting. Developing: states it is in South America. Emerging: vague reference to ‘a poor country’.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a local renewable scheme can reduce poverty.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — reliable electricity replaces costly kerosene, lets children study after dark, allows farmers to refrigerate or grind produce on-site for higher prices, and creates skilled local jobs maintaining the equipment. Uses Chambamontera as evidence. Secure: identifies one effect with explanation. Developing: states the scheme ‘helps people’ without mechanism. Emerging: vague claim.

practice_questions.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of solar and hydro energy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three points of comparison — cost (solar very cheap to install at small scale; hydro expensive at large scale), reliability (solar varies day-to-day; hydro reliable when rain is constant), environmental impact (solar low except for panel production; hydro disrupts ecosystems and may displace communities), location requirements (solar needs sunlight; hydro needs flowing water). Comparative connectives. Secure: two clear comparisons with examples. Developing: lists features of each separately. Emerging: only one feature.

practice_questions.text: Assess how successful the Chambamontera scheme has been at delivering sustainable energy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging successes (around 60 households powered, kerosene replaced, education and incomes improved, locally maintained, 20-year lifespan, no large reservoir) but evaluating limits (only 60 households, only one valley, total cost £43,000 reliant on NGO funding, scheme depends on consistent river flow that climate change may disrupt). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. ‘an excellent local model that needs replicating to have national impact’). Secure: two-sided argument with one or two factors weighed. Developing: lists features with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the tundra growing season?
A) 2–3 months per year
B) 6–10 weeks per year
C) 6–8 months per year
D) Year-round, in short bursts
practice_questions.marks: B) 6–10 weeks per year [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two physical characteristics of cold environments.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per characteristic with development. Examples: extreme low temperatures (tundra winters reach −30°C); permafrost beneath the active surface layer; very low annual precipitation (150–250 mm); thin, waterlogged cryosol soils; short growing season of 6–10 weeks; low angle of sunlight reducing solar radiation.

practice_questions.text: Describe how permafrost affects soils and vegetation in tundra environments.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full chain — permafrost acts as a barrier preventing meltwater draining away; the surface becomes waterlogged; low oxygen slows decomposition so soils stay thin and nutrient-poor (cryosols); only low-growing perennial plants (mosses, sedges, dwarf willows) can survive in such soils; plants grow in cushion shapes to trap warmth near the ground. Secure: two stages with mechanism. Developing: mentions permafrost and plants but no causal link. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain how plants and animals adapt to survive cold environments.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more plant and animal adaptations each linked to the climate. Plants: low cushion growth (avoids wind-chill), dark pigmentation (absorbs weak sunlight), perennial roots (begin growing immediately when active layer thaws). Animals: thick double-layer fur (insulates against extreme cold), counter-current heat exchange in limbs (prevents heat loss), seasonal colour change (camouflage), migration (caribou travel up to 5,000 km following the growing season). Secure: two adaptations per group with explanation. Developing: lists adaptations without reason. Emerging: only one category addressed.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why cold environments have low biodiversity but remain ecologically important.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three linked reasons — low temperatures reduce energy available for life, limiting number of species that can survive; simple food webs (mosses → lemmings → foxes/owls) mean each species depends heavily on the next; losing one species collapses the chain; cold environments store vast carbon reserves in permafrost, so their disruption accelerates global climate change; they regulate ocean currents and Arctic ice reflects solar radiation (albedo). Secure: two reasons explained. Developing: lists features. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: 'Climate change is the greatest threat to biodiversity in cold environments.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with a justified judgement. For: Arctic warming at twice global average rate; permafrost thaw releases methane accelerating warming; phenological mismatch disrupts caribou calving and lemming cycles; polar bear body condition declining as sea-ice season shortens; Arctic summer sea ice projected to disappear before 2050. Against: oil pollution (Exxon Valdez 1989, still traceable 20 years later); invasive species pressure; industrial development destroying habitats; hunting/overfishing. Reaches a judgement — climate change is the most far-reaching threat because it changes the physical foundation of the ecosystem (temperature, permafrost, ice), but pollution and development compound the damage locally. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: generic.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a cause of food insecurity?
A) High crop yields
B) Falling global population
C) Water stress reducing irrigation
D) Declining meat consumption
practice_questions.marks: C) Water stress reducing irrigation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why global food consumption is rising.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: rising global population (world passed 8 billion in 2022, most growth in deficit regions); economic development shifting diets from staple grains to meat and dairy (1 kg of beef requires roughly 7 kg of grain); urbanisation increasing demand for processed food; rising incomes in countries like China increasing per-person calorie consumption.

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of food surplus and deficit.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies surplus regions (North America, Europe, Australasia, parts of South America) with average calorie supply above 3,000 kcal, and deficit regions (sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, parts of Central America) below 2,000 kcal, noting the pattern broadly follows wealth. Secure: identifies the surplus and deficit regions with one named example each. Developing: vague claim about 'rich countries having more food'. Emerging: states there is an unequal distribution without describing the pattern.

practice_questions.text: Explain how conflict can lead to food insecurity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — conflict prevents farmers planting and harvesting, destroys irrigation and storage infrastructure, displaces people from agricultural land, cuts transport routes so food cannot reach markets, and diverts government spending from agriculture to military. Named example: Yemen, South Sudan or Syria. Secure: one clear mechanism with example. Developing: states conflict 'makes farming harder' without mechanism. Emerging: vague link between conflict and food.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how food insecurity can cause social and environmental problems.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points covering both social and environmental — social: price spikes hit poorest households (over 50% of income on food in many African countries); food riots and political instability (Arab Spring 2010–11); chronic undernutrition stunts children's development (149 million children under five). Environmental: over-farming depletes soil (25 billion tonnes of topsoil lost per year); deforestation to open new farmland; over-grazing degrading pasture. Secure: two clear points with evidence, covering at least one social and one environmental. Developing: lists problems without development. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: Assess the extent to which climate is the most important factor affecting food supply.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the power of climate (drought, flooding, extreme heat reducing yields, climate change increasing frequency of extreme events) but weighing it against other factors — conflict (famine in Yemen and South Sudan caused by war, not climate), poverty (farmers lack seeds, tools and credit even in fertile areas), technology (HIC yields 5–10 times higher per hectare than LIC), water stress (70% of global freshwater used in farming), pests and disease (East Africa locust crisis 2020–21 affected 23 million). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. 'climate sets broad boundaries but poverty and conflict turn a poor harvest into a famine'). Secure: two-sided argument with two factors compared. Developing: lists factors with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT one of the three main challenges of developing cold environments?
A) Extreme temperatures
B) Inaccessibility
C) Provision of buildings and infrastructure
D) Lack of mineral resources
practice_questions.marks: D) Lack of mineral resources [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two development opportunities available in Svalbard.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per opportunity with development. Examples: mineral extraction (Mine 7 coal, ~100,000 tonnes per year before its 2025 closure); fishing in the Barents Sea (Arctic cod, haddock, shrimp with international quotas); tourism (around 70,000 visitors per year, cruise ships, wildlife-watching); energy research including the Global Seed Vault (opened 2008, 1.3 million seed samples).

practice_questions.text: Explain why building infrastructure on permafrost is particularly challenging.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — buildings generate heat that melts the permafrost below (thermokarst); soft thawed ground causes subsidence; structures must be raised on piles to avoid this; climate change is already warming Svalbard by around 4°C above 1970s averages, thawing existing permafrost and damaging current buildings; thermosyphons can cool the ground but add cost. Secure: two stages with mechanism. Developing: mentions foundations and permafrost without causal link. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Using a named cold environment, explain the opportunities available for economic development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Svalbard (Norway) named throughout; at least three opportunities explained with mechanism — mineral extraction (Mine 7 coal, ~100,000 tonnes/year before its 2025 closure); fishing (Barents Sea quotas, Arctic cod exported across Europe); tourism (70,000 visitors/year, cruise ships to glaciers and polar bears, UNIS university); energy/science (Global Seed Vault, offshore wind research). Named statistics throughout. Secure: two opportunities with explanation. Developing: opportunities listed without development. Emerging: generic cold environment, no named place.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why cold environments are considered valuable as wilderness areas.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three types of value — scientific (polar ice cores hold 800,000 years of climate data; natural laboratories for studying ecosystems); aesthetic (unspoiled landscapes attract tourists willing to pay); ethical (intrinsic right to exist undisturbed); climate regulation (albedo effect reflects solar radiation; permafrost locks up vast carbon stores); slow recovery (cold slows all processes, so damage is effectively permanent on human timescales). Secure: two types with explanation. Developing: lists benefits. Emerging: 'they are beautiful' alone.

practice_questions.text: 'Economic development and environmental protection cannot coexist in cold environments.' Assess this view using a named example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument using Svalbard throughout with a justified judgement. For the view: cruise ships visit previously undisturbed fjords; coal mining (Mine 7, now closed 2025) contributed to carbon emissions and shows the tension between economic use and environmental goals; Russian operations at Barentsburg difficult to control under the Svalbard Treaty; infrastructure permanently alters the permafrost landscape. Against: Norway's 2002 Environmental Protection Act restricts off-route vehicles; AECO guidelines protect wildlife; directional drilling minimises surface footprint; fishing managed by international quotas preventing overfishing; >65% of Svalbard is protected; the 1991 Madrid Protocol bans extraction in Antarctica entirely. Reaches a judgement that coexistence is possible but requires strong governance, international agreement and technological care — Svalbard demonstrates both successes and tensions. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: generic.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes hydroponics?
A) Growing crops in flooded paddy fields
B) Growing plants in nutrient-rich water without soil
C) Planting crops on hillside terraces
D) Spreading compost to improve soil quality
practice_questions.marks: B) Growing plants in nutrient-rich water without soil [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two advantages of appropriate technology for increasing food supply in LICs.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per advantage with brief development. Examples: low cost means farmers without capital can access it (treadle pumps cost around £25); locally maintained so communities are not dependent on outside expertise; uses readily available materials; long lifespan with minimal running costs; can be implemented quickly without large infrastructure projects.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Makueni sand dam scheme increases food supply.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies the sand dam mechanism (low concrete wall traps sand in a seasonal river, storing water within the sand), how it enables year-round irrigation of vegetable plots, and a specific outcome (multiple harvests per year, over 100,000 people served by 800+ dams in Makueni by 2023). Secure: explains the mechanism and one food-supply outcome. Developing: states it 'provides water for farming' without explaining how. Emerging: vague reference to a 'water scheme in Kenya'.

practice_questions.text: Explain two disadvantages of the Indus Basin Irrigation Scheme.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two disadvantages with full causal explanation — waterlogging and salinity (over-irrigation raises water table, salt crystallises at surface, estimated 6–10 million hectares affected, reducing yields and rendering some land uncultivable); inequity in water distribution (upstream farmers divert excess, tail-reach farmers receive too little); glacial dependence (Himalayan meltwater decline threatens long-term supply). Secure: two disadvantages identified with partial development. Developing: identifies one disadvantage without explanation. Emerging: vague claim that irrigation has problems.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how moving towards sustainable food consumption could reduce global food insecurity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points — reducing waste (one third of food currently lost or wasted; halving this could feed 1 billion more people); seasonal eating cuts carbon and costs of heated greenhouses and air freight, making food cheaper and more accessible; reduced meat consumption (especially beef) releases land and water for other crops; urban farming cuts food miles and improves access for low-income city dwellers (Detroit, Havana, Singapore examples); certified sustainable fish prevents stock collapse. Secure: two developed points with examples. Developing: lists approaches without development. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: Assess how far large-scale agricultural development is the best way to achieve food security.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the scale of large schemes (IBIS feeds 220 million people, provides agricultural export income, supports millions of jobs) but evaluating limits (waterlogging and salinity on 6–10 million hectares, inequitable water distribution, climate risk from glacier retreat, high capital cost). Weighs this against alternatives: sustainable local schemes (Makueni sand dams at £6,000–10,000 each, community-owned, no salinity risk), biotechnology (GM crops increase yield without more land), reducing waste (cheapest route to more effective supply). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. 'large-scale schemes are essential at national scale but only sustainable if complemented by local appropriate technology and consumption change'). Secure: two-sided argument with two factors compared. Developing: describes the IBIS with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes water scarcity?
A) When a country has more water than it needs
B) When water demand exceeds reliable supply
C) When a country transfers water to another
D) When rainfall is seasonal rather than year-round
practice_questions.marks: B) When water demand exceeds reliable supply [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two reasons why global water demand is rising.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per reason with brief development. Examples: rising population (passed 8 billion in 2022, growing fastest in water-scarce regions); economic development (industry, power generation and commercial agriculture need large volumes; higher incomes mean more domestic appliances and longer showers); agricultural expansion (70% of all freshwater withdrawn is used in irrigation).

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern of water surplus and deficit.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies surplus regions (equatorial Africa, Amazon basin, South-East Asia, Scandinavia) where rainfall is heavy and populations relatively small, and deficit regions (Middle East, North Africa, parts of Central Asia, Sahel, northern India) where rainfall is low and/or populations large, noting the pattern is shaped by both physical factors and population pressure. Secure: names one surplus and one deficit region with a reason. Developing: vague claim about 'some countries having more water'. Emerging: states water is unequally distributed without describing a pattern.

practice_questions.text: Explain how over-abstraction can cause water insecurity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full causal chain — pumping groundwater faster than it recharges permanently lowers the water table, drying up wells and springs, eventually making aquifer water unavailable. Specific example: northern India's Punjab water table falling around 1 metre a year; or Saudi Arabia largely depleting fossil aquifers that will not recharge in a human timescale. Secure: identifies the mechanism with one example. Developing: states over-abstraction 'uses up water' without mechanistic explanation. Emerging: vague link between pumping and shortage.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how water insecurity can cause problems for food production and industry.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points covering both sectors — food: irrigated farmland fails as rivers and aquifers run low (California Central Valley fallowing during drought; Sahel shrinking irrigable area); reduced soil moisture cuts rain-fed yields; rising water prices make irrigation unaffordable. Industry: factories and power stations need water for cooling and processing (Indian cities 2019: industries shut as supply failed); thermal power stations cut output; mining and food processing close. Secure: two clear points with examples, covering both food and industry. Developing: lists problems without development. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: Assess the extent to which conflict is the most serious impact of water insecurity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the severity of water conflict (Nile dispute between Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan; UN identifies over 150 potential conflict zones; strategic threat to nations that depend on shared rivers) but evaluating against other impacts — diarrhoeal disease kills around 1.5 million people a year today (direct, immediate and measurable); food production failures cause famine; industrial shutdowns hit economies. Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. 'conflict is a future risk but waterborne disease causes far more deaths today; in the long term, water-driven conflict could be the gravest threat'). Secure: two-sided argument with two impacts compared. Developing: describes impacts with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing evidence.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is formed when three or more corries erode back into a mountain from different sides?
A) An arête
B) A hanging valley
C) A pyramidal peak
D) A truncated spur
practice_questions.marks: C) A pyramidal peak [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline the difference between abrasion and plucking as glacial erosion processes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per process with development. Abrasion: rock fragments embedded in the glacier base grind against bedrock, smoothing and scratching it (leaving striations). Plucking: meltwater at the glacier base freezes around jointed bedrock; as the glacier moves, it tears away blocks of rock — most effective on the downstream side of rock obstacles.

practice_questions.text: Describe the characteristics of a glacial trough.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: clear description of U-shape (flat floor, steep near-vertical sides), broad and straight (interlocking spurs removed, leaving truncated spurs), over-deepened sections that become ribbon lakes (Windermere, 18 km long, 64 m deep), misfit stream on the valley floor. Named UK example (Borrowdale, Nant Gwynant). Secure: U-shape described with two features. Developing: 'wide and deep' only. Emerging: U-shape mentioned but no features.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a corrie is formed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: full sequential explanation — snow accumulates in north/northeast-facing hollow; compacts to glacier ice; rotational slip grinds the floor down by abrasion; backwall steepened by freeze-thaw and plucking; lip eroded less so remains higher; ice retreats leaving tarn (e.g. Red Tarn below Helvellyn, Lake District). At least four stages with processes named. Secure: most stages with process. Developing: rotational slip mentioned but not explained. Emerging: 'the glacier carved it' without process.

practice_questions.text: Suggest reasons why the Lake District's landscape looks very different from a river-eroded landscape.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three contrasts — U-shaped valleys (flat floor, steep sides) vs V-shaped river valleys; truncated spurs vs interlocking spurs; ribbon lakes (Windermere) in over-deepened floors vs no lakes in river valleys; hanging valleys with waterfalls (Aira Force) vs continuous valley floor; corries and arêtes on mountain flanks vs smooth, rounded ridges. Named UK landforms throughout. Secure: two contrasts. Developing: lists landforms without comparison. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: 'Erosion was the dominant process in shaping the UK's glaciated uplands.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument with a justified judgement. For: corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, glacial troughs and ribbon lakes are all erosional landforms dominating the Lake District and Snowdonia skyline; the U-shapes of Borrowdale and Nant Gwynant result entirely from glacial erosion overprinting river valleys. Against: deposition also shaped the landscape — drumlins, moraines and erratics are widespread; the floor of every trough has glacial till; the Cumbrian drumlin field covers vast areas. Also: freeze-thaw weathering (not erosion) shattered the summit ridges and arête crests. Reaches a judgement that erosion is the most visually dominant process in upland cores, but deposition and weathering are equally important on valley floors and lower slopes. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists landforms without judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a ridge of till deposited at the furthest point reached by a glacier?
A) Lateral moraine
B) Medial moraine
C) Terminal moraine
D) Recessional moraine
practice_questions.marks: C) Terminal moraine [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline what makes an erratic distinctive from other glacial deposits.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per point with development. An erratic is a boulder of rock that is completely different from the bedrock it rests on — indicating it was transported by ice from a distant source. Named example: Norber erratics (Yorkshire Dales) — Silurian greywacke boulders on Carboniferous limestone, perched on pedestals up to 50 cm high where the surrounding limestone has been dissolved away.

practice_questions.text: Describe the characteristics of a drumlin.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: asymmetric oval shape; blunt stoss (upstream) end is steep and high; tapered lee (downstream) end points in direction of ice flow; made entirely of unsorted till; found in swarms (basket-of-eggs topography); range from a few metres to 50 m high. Named example (Eden Valley, Cumbria). Secure: shape described with upstream/downstream distinction. Developing: oval and smooth but no asymmetry. Emerging: vague hill description.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between lateral, medial and terminal moraines.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: each type defined, positioned correctly and formation explained — lateral (debris falls from valley walls onto glacier edges, deposited as ridges parallel to old glacier margins); medial (where two glaciers merge, their lateral moraines join to form a central streak, left as a low ridge down the valley floor); terminal (material bulldozed to the snout marks the furthest glacial advance as a curved ridge across the valley). Each type's position and formation clearly linked. Named example for at least one. Secure: two types with explanation. Developing: all three named but poorly defined. Emerging: only one type.

practice_questions.text: Using a named UK upland, identify its major erosional and depositional glacial landforms.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Lake District named throughout; erosional landforms with names — Red Tarn corrie (rotational slip, armchair hollow), Striding Edge arête (two corries eroding back), Windermere ribbon lake (18 km, 64 m deep in glacial trough), Aira Force hanging valley waterfall; depositional — Eden Valley drumlin swarm (streamlined till mounds aligned with ice flow), Norber erratics in the Yorkshire Dales (Silurian greywacke on Carboniferous limestone, perched on pedestal up to 50 cm), terminal and recessional moraines across valley floors. Secure: two erosional and two depositional with names. Developing: names landforms without explanation. Emerging: named area, vague landforms.

practice_questions.text: 'Depositional landforms are as significant as erosional landforms in explaining the landscape of a glaciated upland.' Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument using the Lake District with a justified judgement. For depositional: Eden Valley drumlin swarm covers a vast area; till plains (ground moraine) form the valley-floor farming land; moraines dam ribbon lakes; Norber erratics (Yorkshire Dales) are a striking example of glacial transport. Against: the iconic Lake District views are all erosional — Helvellyn corries, arêtes, glacial troughs, ribbon lakes; the dramatic mountain topography is entirely erosional; deposition is less immediately visible. Reaches a judgement — erosional landforms are more visually dominant in the upland core, but depositional landforms cover a greater total area in the lowland fringe and valley floors and are essential for farming. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: lists landforms without judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a disadvantage of desalination?
A) It can only be used in landlocked countries
B) It produces large amounts of concentrated brine that can harm marine ecosystems
C) It reduces rainfall in nearby areas
D) It requires the displacement of local communities
practice_questions.marks: B) It produces large amounts of concentrated brine that can harm marine ecosystems [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two advantages of water recycling and reuse.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per advantage with brief development. Examples: reduces dependence on rainfall and rivers, increasing resilience to drought (Singapore NEWater meets around 40% of demand); cuts the volume of wastewater discharged, reducing pollution; cheaper than building new dams or desalination plants once infrastructure is in place; Israel recycles over 85% of wastewater for irrigation, the highest rate in the world.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Wakel River Basin johads increased water availability in Rajasthan.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies the johad as an earthen check-dam across a seasonal stream; explains the mechanism (monsoon run-off slowed and spread across land, percolating down to recharge the shallow aquifer); states a specific outcome (groundwater rose by up to 6 metres, dry wells refilled, year-round irrigation became possible, grain yields increased). Secure: explains the mechanism and one outcome. Developing: states johads 'collect water' without explaining how or what changed. Emerging: vague reference to a 'water scheme in India'.

practice_questions.text: Explain two disadvantages of the China South–North Water Transfer Project.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two disadvantages with full causal explanation — displacement (expanding Danjiangkou Reservoir resettled approximately 330,000 people, many with inadequate compensation); ecosystem damage (reduced Yangtze and Han River flow lowered Dongting and Poyang lake levels, threatening endemic species including the Yangtze finless porpoise); cost (estimated 500 billion yuan / £55 billion, reflected in higher consumer water prices); climate risk (source basin rainfall may fall under climate change). Secure: two disadvantages identified with partial development. Developing: identifies one disadvantage without causal explanation. Emerging: vague claim that large schemes cause problems.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how sustainable approaches to water management can reduce water insecurity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three developed points — water conservation reducing demand (Singapore per-person use fell from 165 to 141 litres per day between 2003 and 2020); groundwater management through aquifer recharge slowing depletion (Ogallala Aquifer programmes); recycling and reuse meeting large shares of demand without new rainfall (Singapore 40%, Israel 85%); grey-water systems cheap to install and immediately effective; community rainwater harvesting (johads in Rajasthan raising water table up to 6 metres). Secure: two developed points with examples. Developing: lists approaches without development. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: Assess how far large-scale water transfer schemes are the best solution to water insecurity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the scale of what large transfers achieve (SNWTP supplying over 185 million people, over 60 billion cubic metres transferred by 2023, reducing over-abstraction in the North China Plain) but evaluating costs and limits (£55 billion cost, 330,000 displaced, ecosystem damage, climate risk to source basin). Weighs against alternatives: sustainable approaches (cheaper, lower-impact, community-owned, work with natural cycles — Wakel johads raising groundwater up to 6 metres for minimal cost); conservation (Singapore cutting per-person use through policy alone); recycling (Israel 85% wastewater reuse). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. 'large transfers are necessary at national scale where no alternative can supply cities of millions, but they must be complemented by conservation and recycling to be truly sustainable'). Secure: two-sided argument with two approaches compared. Developing: describes the SNWTP with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which organisation manages footpath restoration in the Lake District under the 'Fix the Fells' project?
A) Natural England
B) The National Trust only
C) The Lake District National Park Authority and partners
D) The Environment Agency
practice_questions.marks: C) The Lake District National Park Authority and partners [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Outline two land use conflicts in a named glaciated upland.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per conflict with development, Lake District named. Examples: walkers vs mountain bikers (bikes damage soft upland paths faster); motorists vs hikers on narrow valley roads; power boats vs canoeists on Windermere (resolved by 10 mph limit, 2005); tourists vs local residents (holiday-cottage demand pushes house prices above local wages, over £300,000 average); quarrying vs conservation (Honister Slate Mine within national park boundary); sheep overgrazing vs habitat recovery.

practice_questions.text: Describe the economic and social impacts of tourism on the Lake District.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: economic — around 18 million visitors per year; £2.4 billion contribution; 16,000 jobs; keeps rural businesses, pubs and hotels viable; farm diversification (B&B, glamping); seasonal employment pattern. Social — house prices inflated by second homes and holiday lets (over £300,000 average); seasonal overcrowding in honeypot villages (Grasmere, Bowness, Keswick); local workers priced out of communities. Named figures throughout. Secure: two impacts per category. Developing: lists impacts without figures. Emerging: only one category.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Lake District attracts so many tourists.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three types of attraction linked to cause — glacially carved landscape (corries, arêtes, U-shaped valleys, ribbon lakes) uniquely concentrated in a small area; England's highest mountain (Scafell Pike, 978 m) draws walkers and climbers; ribbon lakes (Windermere, Ullswater) for water sports and scenic cruises; literary heritage (Wordsworth, Beatrix Potter); UNESCO World Heritage Site status (2017) promotes international tourism; accessibility from major northern cities (Manchester, Leeds, Newcastle). Secure: two attractions with explanation. Developing: lists attractions. Emerging: 'it's beautiful'.

practice_questions.text: Suggest how land use conflicts can be managed in glaciated uplands.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: at least three strategies with the mechanism of how they manage conflict — Fix the Fells (established 2001, path restoration with helicoptered stone, pitching surface to drain water, prevents erosion widening, 400 km restored); 10 mph speed limit on Windermere 2005 (separated powered and quiet water users, reduced noise and waves); park-and-ride at Bowness and Grasmere (reduces car numbers in honeypot villages); agri-environment payments (pay farmers to reduce upland grazing, allowing habitat recovery); planning controls (national park authority must approve new visitor facilities). Each strategy linked to the conflict it resolves. Secure: two strategies explained. Developing: lists strategies. Emerging: vague reference to 'rules'.

practice_questions.text: 'Tourism does more harm than good in glaciated upland areas.' Assess this view using a named example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument using Lake District throughout, with a justified judgement. Against tourism (it does harm): footpath erosion on Striding Edge and Scafell Pike (heavily rutted, widening paths); water pollution from motorised craft and camping; house prices pushed above local wages (over £300,000), pricing out residents; seasonal traffic gridlock on narrow valley roads; disturbance of ground-nesting birds. For tourism (it does good): around 18 million visitors generate £2.4 billion and 16,000 jobs; keeps rural pubs, hotels and services viable; management strategies have worked (Fix the Fells restored 400 km of paths since 2001; 10 mph limit succeeded on Windermere); UNESCO status brings global prestige. Reaches a justified judgement — tourism is essential to the local economy but must be actively managed to avoid long-term environmental damage; the evidence from Fix the Fells shows that good management can reverse harm. Secure: balanced with examples. Developing: one-sided. Emerging: general.
